questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: Listening entails;

options.a: Specifying what a speaker would say
options.b: The ability to identify and understand what a speaker is saying
options.c: Making assertions and statement that guide the speakers speech
options.d: Keeping quite so that the speaker is not distracted

questions.explanation: Listening is the ability to receive, perceive and decode the meaning of spoken words, so B is correct. It is a receptive skill: you take in and understand what the speaker is saying. Options A and C describe the listener acting on the speaker (predicting or guiding the speech), and D, keeping quiet, is just good manners, not listening itself.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: Effective listening requires that;

options.a: The listener dictates the pace and speed of the speakers delivery
options.b: The listener must pay total attention to what the speaker is saying
options.c: The listener interrupts the speaker whenever a point seems wrong
options.d: Examining the speakers attitude and comportment

questions.explanation: Effective listening starts with giving total attention to what the speaker is saying, which is option B. You concentrate on the content and wait for the speaker to finish a point before judging it. Option C is wrong because interrupting breaks your concentration and leads to hasty conclusions, and options A and D focus on controlling or judging the speaker instead of receiving the message.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: The skills involved in listening are;

options.c: Understanding the speaker's accent, vocabulary and presentation of the topic.
options.d: Writing down verbatim everything the speaker says

questions.explanation: Listening is about decoding a spoken message, so the skills involved include understanding the speaker's accent, vocabulary and way of presenting the topic, which is option C. A lecturer's pronunciation and intonation can become barriers, which is why listeners learn to pick up cues like accent and word stress. Options A and B are things you do before the lecture, not listening skills, and D, writing down everything verbatim, is a note-taking habit you should avoid.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: Which of these does not negatively affect listening
questions.explanation: Organized and cohesive speech helps the listener follow the message, so it does not harm listening, and that makes D the answer to this 'does not' question. Listening becomes unproductive because of things like noise in the environment, a speaker's pronunciation problems and the listener's state of mind. Background noise (A), an unfamiliar accent (B) and difficult vocabulary (C) are all barriers, so they do hurt listening.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: All but one of the following are necessary in pre-lecture preparations;

options.a: Conducting surveys of course outlines and topic before hand
options.b: Making intelligent speculations about the lecturers sources
options.c: Arrival at lectures ahead of the lecturer
options.d: A reading of some introductory surveys if the topic is unfamiliar

questions.explanation: Option B is the odd one out: guessing about the lecturer's sources is not part of preparing for a lecture. Good preparation means revising related earlier lectures, reading about the topic, checking the meaning of new key words, and arriving early to sit close to the lecturer. Options A, C and D all match those habits, so they are necessary and cannot be the answer to this 'all but one' question.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: The main goal of a lecture is to;

options.c: Trade information between lecturer and students

questions.explanation: The main goal of a lecture is to impart knowledge to students, which is option B. The lecturer speaks on a subject so that students can capture its essence. Giving a course outline (A) or introducing lecturers (D) are small administrative matters, and C is wrong because a lecture is mostly one-way delivery from lecturer to students, not an equal trade of information.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: Lecturer delivery usually has three parts. These are;

options.b: Outline, main discussion and question time
options.c: Summary, main lecture and expansion of outlined points

questions.explanation: Like any well-organized piece of communication, a lecture has an introduction, a main body and a conclusion, so A is correct. Lecturers even use transition words such as however and consequently to move from one part to the next. Options B and D include items like question time or revision that are not standard parts of the delivery itself, and C wrongly puts a summary at the start.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: One of the following is not a recommended practice in note taking;
questions.explanation: Verbatim recording, option A, is not recommended because you cannot and should not try to write down everything the lecturer says. Instead, reduce the lecture to note form using shorthand, symbols and abbreviations. Options B, C and D (personal abbreviations, logical organization of ideas and summarizing main points) are all good note-taking practices.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: All but one of the following are bad habits in note taking;

options.a: Verbatim recording of everything in note taking
options.b: Recording main points with all the illustration
options.c: Recording main points and a selection of illustrations and examples
options.d: Recording all that the lecturer says

questions.explanation: Good note-taking means separating main points from elaborations, examples and repetitions, and reducing the lecture to compact form. Recording the main points with just a selection of illustrations and examples (option C) does exactly this, so it is the one good habit. Options A and D both mean writing down everything, and B, recording every illustration, defeats the purpose of condensing the lecture.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: Note taking involves the following except;
questions.explanation: Inconsistent personal abbreviations (option B) are not part of good note-taking. You may invent your own symbols and abbreviations, but you must use them consistently, otherwise you will not be able to read your own notes later. Summarizing main points (A), selecting from illustrations (C) and ignoring digressions (D) are all things effective note-takers do.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: A pre-lecture survey is basically

options.a: Asking relevant questions at the beginning of a lecture
options.b: Listening and taking down notes during a lecture
options.c: Reading up on a topic before the lecture
options.d: Discussing a topic with classmates after the lecture

questions.explanation: A pre-lecture survey simply means reading up on a topic before the lecture, so C is correct. It prepares you by giving you background, along with revising earlier related lectures and checking new key terms. Option A happens at the start of the lecture, B during it and D after it, so none of them is done beforehand.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: A course outline is a listing of the

options.a: Specific points raised during a lecture
options.b: Relevant topics to be treated in a particular course
options.c: Form and content of a topic
options.d: Main points articulated during a lecture

questions.explanation: A course outline lists the relevant topics to be treated in a particular course, so B is correct. It is prepared before teaching begins, so it cannot be a record of the specific or main points raised in a lecture (A and D); those belong in lecture notes. Option C, the form and content of a topic, is much narrower than an outline that covers a whole course.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: A good note taken from listening to lecturers is not

options.c: All that is said in class

questions.explanation: A good note is not a record of all that is said in class, so C is the answer. You should not write down everything the lecturer says; good notes use shorthand, abbreviations and summary to capture the main ideas and relevant details. Being brief and concise (A), legible (B) and systematic and orderly (D) are all qualities of good notes, so they are not the answer to this 'is not' question.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: Direct quotation can be distinguished from paraphrase in note taking by

options.c: Writing the quotation in capital letter
options.d: Writing in capital letters as well as underlining it

questions.explanation: When taking notes, a direct quotation is shown by putting it in quotation marks, so B is correct. Short quotations are set within your text and enclosed in double quotation marks. Underlining (A) or writing in capitals (C and D) are not the recognized ways of showing that words are quoted exactly.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: The course outline is usually provided by ____
questions.explanation: The course outline is prepared and handed out by the lecturer who will teach the course, option C, because the lecturer decides which topics will be covered and in what order. The department (A) approves the overall curriculum but does not give out an outline for each course, and course representatives (B) only pass on what the lecturer provides. Since A and B are not sources of the outline, D, all of the above, is also wrong.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: All except the following are included in the course outline of GST105: Use of English
questions.explanation: In this course, GST 105 (now GST 111) covers listening and speaking skills including the sounds of English (phonology), reading and writing skills, grammar, and the use of the library. So A, B and C are all in the outline. Epistemology (option D), the philosophical study of knowledge, is not part of a Use of English course, so it is the exception.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: Which receptive skill involves receiving, perceiving and decoding spoken words?
questions.explanation: Listening is the receptive skill of receiving, perceiving and decoding the meaning of spoken words, so A is correct. Reading (C) is also receptive, but it decodes written symbols, not speech. Speaking (B) and writing (D) are productive skills, since they create language rather than receive it.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: Post-lecture activities include all the following except ------------
questions.explanation: After a lecture you should revise or review your notes quickly, compare them with course-mates, tidy up and fill in missing bits, and try a summary in your own words. Disposal means throwing the notes away, which defeats the purpose of note-taking, so C is the odd one out. Review, summary and revision (A, B and D) are all post-lecture activities.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: Noise is a ---------------- condition.
questions.explanation: Noise is a physical condition, because it belongs to the environment, like a noisy or ill-ventilated room. Listening is hindered by physical conditions of the environment, physiological conditions of the speaker (A, such as speech defects) and psychological conditions of the listener (C, such as emotional state). Option D is not one of these categories.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: Listening is not the ability to ------------------ the meaning of what is being said.
questions.explanation: Listening is the ability to receive, perceive and decode the meaning of what is being said. To denounce means to condemn publicly, which has nothing to do with taking in meaning, so B is the odd one out. A, C and D all describe parts of listening.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: The abbreviation NEC in note-taking means --------------------
questions.explanation: In note-taking, NEC is a shorthand for 'necessary', in the same way that no. stands for number and gov for government. Options B and D read NEC as the initials of an organisation, but that is not its meaning when you are making notes.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: One of the following conditions does not affect listening.
questions.explanation: Three conditions affect listening: the physical condition of the environment, the physiological condition of the speaker and the psychological condition of the listener. Spiritual conditions are not among them, so C is the one that does not affect listening, while A, B and D do.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: Listening to a lecturer does not include -------
questions.explanation: Admiring the lecturer's outfit is a distraction created by dressing, not part of listening, so C is the answer. When listening to a lecturer you should watch for non-verbal cues, observe illustrations and demonstrations, and listen for phonological cues such as voice changes and stress, which are options A, B and D.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: Students are advised to maintain ---------------- contact with their lecturers during classes.
questions.explanation: Maintaining eye contact with your lecturer is the beginning of effective listening, because it links your mind with the speaker's and shows you are ready to process the message. So A is correct. Close contact (D) only suggests sitting near the lecturer, and virtual and full contact (B and C) are not the listening strategy being described.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: During lectures, we engage in ------------------- listening.
questions.explanation: Formal listening takes place in formal or academic settings, so during lectures we engage in formal listening (B). Informal listening (A) happens in everyday conversation and helps relationships. Total and partial listening (C and D) are not recognised types of listening.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: One of the following skills is not necessary in note-taking.
questions.explanation: Sound articulation is a speaking skill, not a note-taking skill, so A is the odd one out. Effective note-taking needs skills such as recognising main ideas, reducing content to note form, sentence reduction, summary and paraphrasing, which are B, C and D.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: Not waiting for the lecture to end before drawing yourconclusion on the content suggests --------------
questions.explanation: Not waiting for the lecture to end before drawing a conclusion is hasty generalisation (A); a good listener is patient enough to let the speaker finish the point before reacting. Emotional attachment (B) refers to prejudice about the topic or lecturer, distraction (C) refers to noise and other interruptions, and mental challenge (D) is actually a positive attitude to adopt.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: A 100L student at UNILAG who is grieving the loss of a relative finds it hard to follow a lecture. Which condition is causing her ineffective listening?

options.a: The linguistic condition of the lecture
options.b: The psychological condition of the listener
options.c: The physiological condition of the lecturer
options.d: The physical condition of the environment

questions.explanation: Grief is an emotional state, and the emotional state or mind of the listener is a psychological condition. The physical condition refers to the environment, such as noise or poor ventilation, not to the listener's feelings.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a purpose of formal listening?

options.a: To analyse a method or step
options.b: To evaluate or criticise a theory or argument
options.c: To improve social relationships in normal conversation
options.d: To remember a formula or concept

questions.explanation: Improving relationships is what informal listening does in normal conversation. Evaluating a theory, remembering a formula and analysing a method are all purposes of formal listening in academic settings such as classes.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: The skill of keeping a record of a speaker's message and recording the essential points from written materials is called
questions.explanation: Note-taking is exactly this: keeping a record of what a speaker says and of the essential points in written texts. Paraphrasing is only one skill used within note-taking, namely restating an idea in your own words.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: To take notes effectively, a student needs skill in which of the following?

options.a: Using a different set of symbols for each lecture
options.b: Writing down only the speaker's examples
options.d: Recording everything the speaker says word for word

questions.explanation: Citing and referencing the works you use correctly is one of the six requirements for effective note-taking. Recording everything word for word is wrong because effective note-taking reduces content to a short, summarised form and avoids verbatim writing.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: A lecturer in a firm's training session in Ikeja first explains what drives inflation in Nigeria and then explains what inflation does to households. Which organising principle is the lecture following?
questions.explanation: Moving from what produces something to what it leads to is the cause-and-result organising principle. Problem and solution would require the speaker to propose remedies, which this talk does not do.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: While listening to a lecture, words such as 'in addition', 'however', 'moreover' and 'consequently' should be noted as
questions.explanation: These connecting words are transition cues that show how the speaker's ideas link and where the talk is heading. Phonological cues are features of the voice, such as accent, stress and speed, not linking words.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: During a lecture, changes in the lecturer's voice, accent, word stress and speed are examples of
questions.explanation: Features carried by the sound of the voice, such as accent, word stress, speed and emotional nuance, are phonological cues. Non-verbal cues are different because they are seen, not heard: facial expressions, gestures and body movement.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: Which of the following is an AFTER-lecture activity for effective note-taking?

options.a: Checking new words related to the topic
options.b: Preparing the format of your notes
options.c: Arriving early and sitting close to the lecturer
options.d: Comparing your notes with those of course-mates

questions.explanation: Comparing what you wrote with course-mates soon after the class helps you fill in gaps. Arriving early and sitting close to the speaker is a step taken before the class, as are checking new words and preparing the format you will write in.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: In note-taking, the abbreviation 'c.f.' stands for
questions.explanation: 'c.f.' means confer, that is, compare one point with another. 'That is' is written as 'i.e.', 'note well' as 'NB' and 'including' as 'incl.'.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: A student deliberately ignores her tribal and religious bias against a guest lecturer so that she can follow his argument. Which listening strategy is she applying?

options.c: Treating listening as a mental challenge

questions.explanation: Putting aside religious, cultural, tribal or financial bias and personal emotions is the strategy of suppressing emotional attachment. Avoiding hasty generalisations is about waiting for the speaker to finish before drawing conclusions, which is a different strategy.

questions.topic: Listening Skills and Note-taking
questions.question: When taking notes, where should you write your own thoughts about what the lecturer is saying?

options.a: Mixed in with the lecturer's main points
options.b: In a separate column or in the margin
options.c: In a separate notebook kept at home
options.d: Nowhere, because personal thoughts are not allowed

questions.explanation: Your own thoughts should be added in a separate column or in the margin so that they stay distinct from the speaker's points. Mixing them in with the main points makes it hard to tell later which ideas came from the speaker.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: Phonetics is to pronunciation what ---------------- is to spelling.
questions.explanation: Phonetics is the systematic study of how words are pronounced, and orthography, option D, is the conventional system of spelling words in a language, so the two are parallel. Syntax (A) deals with sentence structure and semantics (B) with meaning, while interpretation (C) is not a branch of language study, so none of them relates to spelling.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: The symbol ':' used alongside a phonetic symbol suggests ----------------
questions.explanation: A colon-like mark written after a vowel symbol is a length mark showing that the vowel is long, as in the contrast between /i:/ in seat and /I/ in sit, so C is correct. It changes only the length, not the quality of the sound. Aspiration (D) and labialisation (A) are different features of consonants, and colony (B) is not a phonetic term at all.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: The word 'youth' can be transcribed as ------------------
questions.explanation: Youth begins with the palatal glide /j/ (the sound spelt y), followed by the long vowel /u:/ as in food, and ends with the voiceless th sound /θ/, so A is correct. Options C and D wrongly use the letter y instead of the phonetic symbol /j/, and options B and D end in the voiced /ð/ of this and mother, which is not the sound in youth.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: One of the following is not a distinction made between vowels.
questions.explanation: Vowels are described by tongue height (high/low), openness (close/open), length (long/short, also called tense/lax) and lip shape, where the lips may be spread, neutral or rounded. Rounded contrasts with spread or neutral, never with 'around', which is not a phonetic term, so A is the one that is not a real distinction. Options B, C and D are all genuine pairs.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: /s/ /t/ and /n/ are related based on their --------------- of articulation.
questions.explanation: The sounds /s/, /t/ and /n/ are all alveolar, made with the tip or blade of the tongue touching the alveolar ridge behind the upper teeth, so what they share is place of articulation. Option B (manner) is wrong because their manners differ: /s/ is a fricative, /t/ a stop and /n/ a nasal. Nature and length are not ways of describing consonants.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: There are -------------- sounds altogether in English.
questions.explanation: English has forty-four significant sounds (phonemes): twenty vowels and twenty-four consonants, so C is correct. Options A (20) and D (24) are only the vowel count and the consonant count on their own, and B (26) is the number of letters in the alphabet. Letters and sounds do not correspond one to one.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: The term 'lateral' refers to -----------------
questions.explanation: A lateral consonant is made when the tip of the tongue touches the alveolar ridge and air escapes along the sides of the tongue, and that sound is /l/. Option A (/r/) is a post-alveolar approximant, while C and D (/j/ and /w/) are glides, a sub-group of approximants.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: The airstream that is used for the production of most English sounds is the ----------- ------ airstream.
questions.explanation: The lungs provide the airstream for most speech, and this air pushed out from the lungs is called the pulmonic egressive airstream. Option A (laryngeal) names where the vocal folds are rather than an airstream, while C and D (glottalic, velaric) are other airstream mechanisms used in some languages but not for ordinary English sounds.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: Which of the following words contains three sounds?
questions.explanation: Cheap has three sounds because the ch is a single affricate consonant, as in church, followed by the long vowel in seat and then p. The other words have more: trust (A) has five sounds, frog (C) has four, and thoughts (D) has four (th, the vowel, t, s), so only B fits.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the lip positions used to describe English vowels?
questions.explanation: English vowels are described by three lip positions: spread (as in seat), neutral (as in cup) and rounded (as in food). Pursed is not one of these positions, so C is correct, while A, B and D are all genuine lip positions.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: --------------- combines the manner of articulation of stops and fricatives.
questions.explanation: Affricates begin like plosives (stops) and end like fricatives: the airflow is first blocked completely and then released gradually with friction, as in the first sounds of church and judge. Option D is wrong because nasals start with a closure but release air through the nose, and A is wrong because glides are approximants with no closure and no friction.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: High vowels are also described as -------------------- vowels.
questions.explanation: When the tongue is held up close to the roof of the mouth, high vowels such as /i:/ and /u:/ are produced, and these are also called close vowels, so D is correct. Option C (open) is the opposite, since low vowels are open, and A and B describe length and lip shape, not tongue height.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: -------------------- is not a bilabial sound.
questions.explanation: Bilabial sounds are made with the two lips coming together, as in /p/, /b/, /m/ and /w/. The sound /f/ is labio-dental, made with the lower lip touching the upper front teeth, so D is not bilabial, while A, B and C are.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: One of the following is not involved in vowel articulation
questions.explanation: Vowels are produced with no obstruction to the airflow, so the articulators do not touch each other; that is why contact (D) is not involved in vowel articulation. Contact belongs to consonants. Tongue movement, lip shaping and length (A, B and C) are all used to describe vowels, so they are not the odd one out.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: ----------------- is the high, back tense vowel.
questions.explanation: /u:/ is the high, back, tense vowel, heard in words like rule, food and who. Option D, /i:/, is also high and tense but it is a front vowel, A is a central vowel, and B is low and back.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: Vowel distinctions do not include:
questions.explanation: English vowels are divided into pure vowels or monophthongs (12) and diphthongs (8), and triphthongs are also mentioned when discussing strong syllables. There is no class called quadriphthongs in English phonology, so C is the odd one out, while A, B and D are genuine vowel distinctions.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: Symbols used in phonetic transcription are adapted from -----------------
questions.explanation: The symbols used to represent English sounds are adapted from the International Phonetic Association's alphabet, usually called the IPA (C). APA and MLA (B and D) are referencing styles, not phonetic systems, and PLA (A) is not a recognised source of phonetic symbols.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: The lungs are housed in the -------------------------
questions.explanation: The lungs are sponge-like tissues housed in the rib cage, and they provide the airstream used for speech (D). The larynx (C) is tempting because it is part of the airway, but it houses the vocal folds, not the lungs. The pharynx (B) is part of the throat above the larynx, and the spinal cord (A) is part of the nervous system.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: Voicing occurs as a result the ------------------ of the vocal folds.
questions.explanation: Voicing happens when the glottis is relatively closed and the vocal folds vibrate under air pressure from the lungs, so the answer is vibration (B). Separation (C) describes the open glottis that produces voiceless sounds, and agitation and relaxation (A and D) are not the terms used for voicing.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: ---------------- is a glottal sound.
questions.explanation: /h/ is a voiceless glottal fricative, made with friction at the glottis, the gap between the vocal folds (C). /k/ (A) is a voiceless velar stop made with the back of the tongue against the soft palate. /w/ (B) is a bilabial glide and /j/ (D) is a palatal glide, so neither is made at the glottis.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: Of the 20 vowel sounds of English, how many are pure vowels (monophthongs)?
questions.explanation: English has 20 vowels made up of 12 pure vowels and 8 diphthongs. The figure 8 is the number of diphthongs, not of pure vowels.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: How many diphthongs are there in English?
questions.explanation: English has 8 diphthongs, made up of 5 closing diphthongs and 3 centring diphthongs. The figure 5 counts only the closing group, not all the diphthongs.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: How many of the English diphthongs are closing (rising) diphthongs?
questions.explanation: Five of the eight diphthongs are closing: they start with a mid or low element and glide to a high one. The other 3 are the centring diphthongs, which end in the schwa.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: The centring diphthongs of English are so called because they all end in
questions.explanation: A centring diphthong glides towards the centre of the mouth and ends in the schwa. Ending in a high vowel is what marks the closing diphthongs instead.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: How many consonant phonemes does English have?
questions.explanation: Of the 44 English phonemes, 24 are consonants and 20 are vowels. The figure 44 is the total of all sounds, not the consonants alone.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the parameters for describing English consonants?
questions.explanation: Consonants are described by place of articulation, manner of articulation and the state of the glottis (voicing). Lip rounding is one of the parameters used for vowels, not consonants.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: English vowels are described WITHOUT reference to which of the following?
questions.explanation: Vowels are described by tongue height, tongue horizontality, lip rounding and duration, not by place or manner. Manner of articulation belongs to consonants, which involve an obstruction of the airflow.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: When the glottis is wide open so that air passes freely through it, the sound produced is
questions.explanation: An open glottis lets the air through without making the vocal folds vibrate, so the sound is voiceless. A voiced sound needs the glottis nearly closed so that the folds vibrate.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: The gap between the vocal folds is called the
questions.explanation: The glottis is the space between the two vocal folds. The larynx is the structure that houses the vocal folds, not the gap between them.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: Which articulator is a muscular flap that is raised to shut off the nasal tract?
questions.explanation: The soft palate (velum) is the muscular flap that rises to close off the nose. The hard palate is the bony front part of the roof of the mouth and cannot move.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: Which of the following is the most flexible articulator?
questions.explanation: The tongue is the most flexible articulator, with parts such as the tip, blade, front, centre, back and root. The lips are also active articulators, but they are less flexible than the tongue.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: Which of the following is a passive (fixed) articulator?
questions.explanation: Passive articulators do not move; the teeth and the hard palate are the fixed ones. The soft palate looks close to the hard palate but it is movable, so it is an active articulator.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: Consonants produced with a closure in the mouth and the velum lowered, so that the air escapes through the nose, are called
questions.explanation: Nasals such as /m/ and /n/ block the mouth while the lowered velum lets the air out through the nose. A lateral, such as /l/, lets the air pass along the sides of the tongue instead.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: The approximants /w/ and /j/ form the sub-group of sounds known as
questions.explanation: /w/ and /j/ are the glides within the approximant class. Liquids is the name given to /l/ and /r/ together.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: Taken together, the consonants /l/ and /r/ are known as
questions.explanation: /l/ and /r/ are grouped together as the liquids. The glides are /w/ and /j/, a different sub-group.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: Using the order voicing, place, manner, the English consonant /p/ is described as a
questions.explanation: /p/ is made with both lips (bilabial), with total closure and sudden release (stop), and without vibration of the vocal folds (voiceless). A voiced bilabial stop describes /b/, the voiced partner of /p/.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: The consonants /f/ and /v/ share the same place of articulation, which is
questions.explanation: /f/ and /v/ are made with the lower lip against the upper teeth, so they are labio-dental. Bilabial sounds use both lips, as in /p/, /b/ and /m/.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: Which pair of English consonants is velar?
questions.explanation: /k/ and /g/ are made with the back of the tongue against the soft palate (velum), so they are velar. /t/ and /d/ are also stops, but they are alveolar.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: The fact that the letter 'a' is pronounced differently in 'gate', 'woman', 'many' and 'village' shows that

options.a: each English letter has one fixed sound
options.c: the letter 'a' is always a diphthong
options.d: English has little or no sound-letter correspondence

questions.explanation: The same letter stands for different sounds in these words, so English spelling does not match its sounds closely. That is why spelling cannot be trusted to show how a word is pronounced.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills I: Sounds of English
questions.question: How many sounds are there in the word 'trust'?
questions.explanation: 'trust' has five sounds: /t/, /r/, the short vowel heard in 'cut', /s/ and /t/. A common mistake is to count 4 by treating the cluster 'tr' or 'st' as a single sound.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: 'humble:
questions.explanation: Humble is stressed on the first syllable (HUM-ble), and standard (STAN-dard), option C, has the same pattern. Report (re-PORT), regret (re-GRET) and return (re-TURN), options A, B and D, all carry their stress on the second syllable, so they do not match.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: Com'plaint:
questions.explanation: Complaint is stressed on the second syllable (com-PLAINT), and success (suc-CESS), option A, has the same pattern. Saddle (SAD-dle), punish (PUN-ish) and marvel (MAR-vel), options B, C and D, are all stressed on the first syllable.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: con'cern
questions.explanation: Concern is stressed on the second syllable (con-CERN), and the verb combine (com-BINE) has the same pattern, so B is correct. Pretext (PRE-text), concert (CON-cert) and comment (COM-ment) are all stressed on the first syllable. Concert may look tempting because it starts with con- like concern, but as a noun its stress falls on the first syllable.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: pro'fessor
questions.explanation: Professor has its stress on the second syllable (pro-FES-sor), and creator (cre-A-tor) has the same pattern, so A is correct. Activist (AC-ti-vist), company (COM-pa-ny) and minister (MIN-is-ter) all take their stress on the first syllable, so they do not match.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: indi'cation
questions.explanation: Indication has four syllables with the main stress on the third (in-di-CA-tion), and education (ed-u-CA-tion) follows the same pattern, so C is correct. Words ending in -tion usually take their stress on the syllable just before the ending. Ambition (am-BI-tion) and reaction (re-AC-tion) have only three syllables, and competitor (com-PE-ti-tor) is stressed on the second syllable, so none of them matches.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: 'capitalism
questions.explanation: Capitalism takes its main stress on the first syllable (CAP-i-tal-ism), and regionalism (RE-gion-al-ism) has the same pattern, so C is correct. The suffix -ism does not move the stress, so each word keeps the stress of its base (capital, region). Occurrence (oc-CUR-rence), insurance (in-SUR-ance) and development (de-VEL-op-ment) are all stressed on the second syllable.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: Affixes which cause stress to move from one syllable to another are known as -------- --------------- affixes.
questions.explanation: Affixes that shift the stress to a different syllable of the stem are called stress-moving affixes, option C, for example -ic and -ity, as in MAGnet becoming magNETic and INfidel becoming infiDELity. Stress-neutral affixes (B) leave the original stress unchanged, like un- in unPLEASant, and stress-bearing affixes (D) carry the stress themselves, like -eer in engiNEER. Stress-conserving (A) is not a standard term.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: A maximum of --------------- consonants are permissible at the beginning of an English syllable.
questions.explanation: The structure of the English syllable is C0-3 V C0-4, so the onset (the consonants before the vowel) can hold up to three consonants, as in spree, straw and sprint. That makes A, 3, correct. Options B, C and D (4, 5, 6) exceed the limit; four consonants are possible only at the end of a syllable, as in strengths.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: -eer in 'engineer' and -aire in 'millionaire' are examples of -------------------- affixes.
questions.explanation: Stress-bearing affixes are the ones that carry the primary stress themselves, as -eer does in engineer and -aire does in millionaire, so C is correct. A (stress-neutral) affix leaves the stress where it was, B (stress-moving) shifts stress to another syllable of the stem, and D (stress-conserving) is not a recognised category.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: An affix which does not affect the position of stress in a word is ---------------
questions.explanation: A stress-neutral affix does not change where the stress falls: the word keeps its original stress, as in pleasant and unpleasant, or market and marketing. Option B (stress-bearing) means the affix itself takes the stress, D (stress-moving) shifts it to another syllable, and C (stress-conserving) is not a recognised category.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: One of the following is not a criterion for predicting stress.
questions.explanation: Stress placement in English words can be predicted using phonological criteria (the structure of the syllables), syntactic criteria (the word class, as in REcord versus reCORD) and morphological criteria (the effect of affixes). Semantic criteria, that is, meaning, are not used, so D is correct, and A, B and C are genuine criteria.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: The word 'challenge' when used as a noun or a verb is respectively stressed as----------------
questions.explanation: In this course, challenge is treated as an exception to the noun-verb stress rule: unlike EXport/exPORT or REcord/reCORD, it keeps the same stress pattern, CHALlenge, whether it is a noun or a verb. Options A and D wrongly assume the stress shifts between the two uses, and C has the wrong stress for both.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: Zero stress refers to:
questions.explanation: Zero stress refers to unstressed syllables, such as the first syllable of about or the last syllable of mother. Polysyllabic words have three levels: primary, secondary and zero stress. Options C and D are the other two levels, which do carry some prominence, and B (tertiary) is not a level used in this course.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: Which stress level is marked with a subscript?
questions.explanation: Secondary stress is weaker than primary stress but stronger than an unstressed syllable, and it is marked with a subscript mark at the start of the syllable, as in the first syllable of millionaire or cigarette. Option C (primary) is marked with a raised stroke, B (zero stress) has no mark at all, and D (tertiary) is not a level used here.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: The syllable in a word which has a --------------------- vowel quality usually attracts stress.
questions.explanation: A syllable with a strong vowel quality (a long vowel, diphthong or triphthong) tends to attract stress, while syllables with weak vowels such as the schwa are usually unstressed. Options A, C and D describe tongue height or lip shape, not whether a vowel is strong or weak, so they do not predict stress.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: English stress is -----------------
questions.explanation: English stress is free, meaning it is not tied to one fixed position, so it can fall on the first, second, third or last syllable of a word, unlike languages where stress is fixed. Option A (fixed) is therefore the direct opposite of the right answer, and B and C are not terms used to describe stress systems.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: Which of the following is a compound noun?
questions.explanation: Compound nouns carry stress on the first element, so GREENhouse (a glass building for plants) is a compound noun, whereas a green HOUSE, with stress on the second word, is just a noun phrase meaning a house that is green. Options B, C and D all stress the second element, which is the noun-phrase pattern.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: Stress prediction based on syllable structure is basically ----------------
questions.explanation: The phonological criterion predicts stress from the number of syllables in a word and their internal structure, especially whether they contain strong or weak vowels, so C is correct. Option B (morphological) is based on affixes and word parts, A (syntactic) is based on word class, and D (semantic) is about meaning, so none of them concerns syllable structure.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: ---------------- is the use of the rise and fall of voice pitch to convey meaning.
questions.explanation: Intonation is the melody of speech: the rise and fall of pitch used to show meaning, such as whether a sentence is a statement or a question, or the speaker's attitude. Option B (stress) is the prominence of one syllable over others in a word, and C and D (rhythm, intensity) are not the names for meaningful pitch movement.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: Which of the following statements is not correct?

options.a: noun phrases are stressed on the rightmost constituent
options.b: compound nouns are usually stressed on the first constituent

questions.explanation: Statement D is incorrect because function words such as the, of and and are usually unstressed in connected speech, not always stressed. The other statements are correct: noun phrases are stressed on the rightmost element (A), compound nouns on the first element (B), and content words like nouns normally carry stress (C).

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: One of the following is not necessary to make a syllable prominent.
questions.explanation: Four factors make a syllable prominent: loudness, length, pitch and vowel quality. Voice, meaning vocal fold vibration, is what separates sounds like /b/ and /p/, and it is not a feature of stress, so B is not necessary. A, C and D are all prominence factors.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: The ------------------ is the only compulsory element in a syllable.
questions.explanation: A syllable has an onset, a peak and a coda. The onset and coda (consonants) are optional, while the peak, which contains a vowel, is compulsory, so A is correct. Option C is wrong because a syllable like I or eye has no consonant at all, and B and D are word classes, not parts of a syllable.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: ---------------------, according to experts, produces the strongest effect on stress placement than all the other features.
questions.explanation: Pitch produces the strongest effect on stress placement of all the prominence factors, so C is correct. Length (A), loudness (B) and vowel quality (D) also contribute to prominence, but none is as powerful as a noticeable change in pitch.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: Features which apply to units higher than the segments are known as ---------
questions.explanation: Features such as stress and intonation operate on the syllable and beyond, not on individual consonant and vowel segments, so they are called suprasegmentals, meaning above the segments. Option C (segmentals) refers to the individual sounds themselves, and A and B are not terms used in phonology for this.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: The ------------ criterion for stress prediction takes the internal structure of the word into consideration.
questions.explanation: The morphological criterion for stress looks at the internal structure of a word, whether it is simple, compound or complex and what affixes it carries, so D is correct. Option B (phonological) looks at syllable and vowel structure, A (syntactic) looks at word class, and C (semantic) is about meaning, so none of them is about the word's internal make-up.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: The prominence of one syllable over other syllables in a word is a function of ...
questions.explanation: Stress is the relative prominence of one syllable over the others in a word, so A is correct. Pitch, length and intensity (B, C and D) are the features that create that prominence, but the prominence itself is what we call stress.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: In the word 'janitor', stress falls on the ------------------- syllable.
questions.explanation: Janitor is stressed on the first syllable, so it is said JAnitor, just like reason and message. That makes the answer initial (A). Options B and C would move the stress to -i- or -tor, which is not how the word is pronounced.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: A three consonant onset obligatorily has -------------- as the first consonant.
questions.explanation: A three-consonant onset always starts with /s/, followed by /p/, /t/ or /k/ and then /l/, /r/, /w/ or /j/, as in strike, square and sprite. So B is correct. Options A, C and D (/k/, /t/, /p/) are the sounds that can come second, not first.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: One of the following does not usually occur in unstressed syllables.
questions.explanation: Diphthongs are strong vowels that attract stress, so they do not normally appear in unstressed syllables (D). The schwa and syllabic consonants usually occur in unstressed syllables, and weak syllables contain short vowels, which is why A, B and C are not the answer.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: A word usually has --------------- primarily-stressed syllable(s).
questions.explanation: In longer words there is usually just one primarily stressed syllable, possibly one more with secondary stress, and several unstressed ones. So a word normally has one primary stress (B). Options A, C and D give too many; extra prominent syllables carry secondary stress, not primary stress.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: The ------------------ tune is used in declarative sentences.
questions.explanation: The falling tune is used in declarative statements, as well as in commands, wh-questions and exclamations (D). The rising tune (B) is used for yes/no questions and polite requests, the fall-rise (A) is for lists and sentence modifiers, and the rise-fall (C) is not the tune linked with statements.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: When the intonation of a sentence identifies that sentence as a statement, question etc. it is said to perform a/an ------------------ function.
questions.explanation: Showing whether an utterance is a statement, a question or an exclamation is the grammatical function of intonation (A). The attitudinal function (B) reveals the speaker's emotion or attitude, and the discourse function (D) guides turn-taking in conversation. Accentual (C) relates to stress placement, not sentence type.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: A syllable with a CV structure is said to be ----------------------
questions.explanation: A CV syllable ends in a vowel, so it has no coda and is an open syllable (D), like the words tea and slow. Closed syllables (A) end in a consonant, as in CVC. Strong and weak (B and C) describe the vowel quality in a syllable, not its structure.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: Yes/No questions are naturally asked using the ........................ tune.
questions.explanation: The rising tune is used to ask yes/no (polar) questions, as in 'Can we go now?' (A). The falling tune (C) is used for statements, commands and wh-questions, the fall-rise (B) is for lists and sentence modifiers, and the rise-fall (D) is not linked with yes/no questions.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: The word 'responsibility' is correctly stressed as ------------
questions.explanation: Responsibility has primary stress on the fourth syllable, bil, and secondary stress on the second syllable, so the correct marking is responsi'bility (C). Option D, re'sponsibility, is tempting because the base word responsible is stressed there, but the suffix -ity moves the primary stress to the syllable just before it.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: -------------- is the use of the pitch of the voice to convey meaning or syntactic information.
questions.explanation: Intonation is the use of the pitch of the voice to convey meaning or syntactic information (B). Stress (C) is the extra prominence given to one syllable within a word, rhythm (A) is the timing pattern of speech, and phonetics (D) is the study of speech sounds as a whole.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: The theory that a syllable corresponds to one puff of air from the intercostal muscles is the
questions.explanation: The Chest Pulse Theory links each syllable to a single puff of air pushed out by the intercostal muscles. The Prominence Theory instead defines the syllable by the most prominent or sonorous sound in its environment.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: Which of the following words is a closed syllable?
questions.explanation: A closed syllable ends in a consonant (a coda), and 'slap' ends in /p/. 'slow', 'tea' and 'no' all end in a vowel sound, so they are open syllables.

questions.topic: Speaking Skills II: Syllable, Stress, Intonation
questions.question: A student asks a stranger, 'Where is the Faculty of Management Sciences?' to get new information. Which tune is normally used?
questions.explanation: Wh-questions that seek new information are said on a falling tune. A rising tune is used for yes/no questions and for wh-questions that ask someone to repeat what was said, which is not the case here.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: Selective reading is important to students because

options.a: It will be in line with qualitative education
options.b: It reduces the stress campus rigors
options.c: It may be either impossible or a waste of time to read everything in the text
options.d: It reinforces the importance of reading

questions.explanation: Selective reading matters because it may be impossible, or a waste of time, to read everything in a text, so C is correct. Believing you must read every word is a misconception; depending on your purpose and how familiar the material is, you can read selectively. Options A, B and D give vague benefits that do not explain the real reason.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: The main purpose of reading is to \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ a written material.
questions.explanation: The main purpose of reading is to comprehend written material, so B is correct. The eyes link letters and symbols to see what the author says, while the brain interprets what the author means, and the goal of study reading is understanding and retaining the material. Practising (A), identifying (C) and buying (D) are not what reading itself is for.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: ------------------- is the process of translating written or printed symbols and letters into words and sentences which convey meaning.
questions.explanation: Reading is the process of translating written or printed symbols and letters into words and sentences which convey meaning, using both the eyes and the brain, so C is correct. Listening (A) decodes spoken words rather than written symbols, while speaking (B) and writing (D) are productive skills that create language rather than interpret it.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: ---------------------- is not a key element to look out for when reading a material.
questions.explanation: When reading with intent, the key elements to look for are the meaning of the title and subtitles, the introduction, the author's main point (thesis statement), the supporting explanation and the conclusion. Spelling errors are not among them; hunting for them is proofreading, not reading for understanding. A, B and C are all key elements, so D is the exception.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: One of the following is not a type of reading.
questions.explanation: The types of reading are skimming (quick reading for the overall idea), scanning (searching for a specific piece of information) and study reading (intensive, critical reading). Spinning is not a reading technique at all, so A is the odd one out, and B, C and D are all genuine types.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: Skimming can be classified under---------------
questions.explanation: Efficient reading has three stages: preview before reading, read with intent, and review after reading. Skimming gives you the overall idea and familiarises you with the content and organisation, so it belongs to the preview stage, which is why you should not start reading without skimming first. Option D (reading with intent) involves searching for key elements and highlighting, and C (review) comes after reading.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: In reviewing an item you have read, one of the following is not necessary.
questions.explanation: When you review material after reading, you pay attention to the heading, the highlighted or underlined items that point to the main ideas, and the annotated items in the margin. The author's references are not part of this review, so C is the one that is not necessary, while A, B and D are the three items you should look at.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: In scanning a reading material. the reader seeks to --------------------

options.c: have a general idea of the topic

questions.explanation: In scanning, your eyes run quickly through a text looking for a particular piece of information, ignoring everything not relevant to it, so A is correct. Option C (a general idea of the topic) describes skimming, not scanning, and B and D (grammaticality, plagiarism) are not purposes of reading at all.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: When our eyes make a backward movement during reading, it is known as ---------- ----------
questions.explanation: Regression is glancing back to re-read words, phrases or sentences, usually because of poor concentration, and it is counted among bad reading habits. Options A, B and C (clearing, backwarding, forwarding) are not terms used for eye movement in reading.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: The mnemonic -------------------- serves as a guide to productive study reading.
questions.explanation: LEARNER is the mnemonic that guides productive study reading: Lay out the purpose, Examine all parts, Ask questions about each subheading, Read all materials on the topic, Note names, places and dates, Ease away from one subject before starting another, and Review before a test. Options B, C and D are not study-reading mnemonics.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: In scanning, the -------------------- can be very important.
questions.explanation: When you scan, you are hunting for one particular piece of information, so you use the table of contents or the index to find the relevant pages and then read only those. Preface and foreword (A and C) are introductory sections that help with skimming, not with locating a specific fact, and topic sentences (D) help you understand paragraphs rather than find a detail quickly.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: --------------------- is not a bad reading habit.

options.c: moving the head from side to side

questions.explanation: Having a wide span of recognition is a mark of a good reader, because the eyes take in several words at one fixation, so D is not a bad habit. Word-by-word reading, vocalisation and moving the head from side to side (B, A and C) are all reading deficiencies that slow you down and hurt comprehension.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: You will not experience much difficulty with a reading material if you ---------------
questions.explanation: You will not struggle much with a reading material if you follow the appropriate steps, such as previewing, reading with intent and reviewing (A). Options B, C and D are the usual causes of difficulty, namely a confusing style, not connecting with the author and an uninteresting topic, so they are the opposite of what the question asks for.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: Skimming involves the following except------------------

options.d: looking at the table of contents

questions.explanation: Looking for specific details is scanning, not skimming, so A is the exception. In skimming you look at the title, blurb, abstract, table of contents and topic sentences to get a general idea, without hunting for particular facts, which is why B, C and D are all part of skimming.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: The reading speed adopted depends on all the following except ---------------------------

options.a: the nature of the reading material

questions.explanation: The nature of the reading material and your purpose decide how thoroughly and how fast you read, and a flexible reader changes speed to suit the material, so A, B and C all matter. The author does not prescribe how fast you read, so D is the odd one out.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: One of the following is NOT essential to reading
questions.explanation: Reading is translating written or printed symbols into meaning, and it involves the eyes and the brain. The articulatory system (lips, tongue, vocal cords) is not needed, and moving the vocal organs while reading is actually a bad habit called vocalisation, so C is the answer. Printed signs, the eyes and written signs (A, B and D) are all essential.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: By the end of a university programme, a student's reading speed should be about
questions.explanation: The target for reading efficiency is about 600 words per minute by the end of your programme, and it improves only with practice. Lower figures such as 300 words per minute fall well short of this target.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: The relationship between the physical aspect of reading and reading speed, which in turn affects comprehension, is known as
questions.explanation: Reading efficiency means having the right skills for efficient physical and mental processing, linking the physical act of reading to speed and comprehension. Span of recognition is narrower: it is only how many words you take in at each eye fixation.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: A student in Lagos accepts every claim in a newspaper simply because it has been printed. Which misconception about reading does she hold?

options.a: Everything can be read the same way
options.d: Everything on a page is equally important

questions.explanation: Trusting a claim just because it is printed is the misconception that everything in print is true; a critical reader separates facts from opinions. Believing that everything on a page is equally important is a different misconception, about what to focus on rather than what to believe.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four misconceptions about reading?

options.a: Everything can be read the same way
options.b: Reading speed is related to comprehension
options.c: Everything on a page is equally important

questions.explanation: Scholars agree that reading speed is directly related to comprehension, so this is a true statement, not a misconception. Believing that you must read everything is one of the four false ideas.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: A reader who moves his lips or whispers the words while reading silently has the bad habit called
questions.explanation: Moving the lips or vocal apparatus, or whispering, is vocalisation. Sub-vocalisation is close but different: the words are pronounced only in the mind with no movement.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: Pronouncing words in the mind while reading, without any movement of the lips, is called
questions.explanation: Sub-vocalisation is saying the words silently in the mind, and it slows reading down. Vocalisation involves visible lip movement or whispering, which is not happening here.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: A reader who recognises only one or two words at each eye fixation has
questions.explanation: Taking in only one or two words per fixation is a short span of recognition, a bad habit; a good reader has a wide span. Erratic eye movement is about the eyes failing to move rhythmically from phrase to phrase.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: To avoid erratic eye movement, a reader's eyes should move

options.a: along the line by following a pointing finger
options.b: together with the head from side to side
options.c: from the first letter of each word to the next
options.d: rhythmically from the middle of one phrase to the middle of the next

questions.explanation: Good readers move their eyes in a steady rhythm from the middle of one phrase to the middle of the next. Following a pointing finger is itself a bad habit, and moving the head is another, since only the eye muscles should be used.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: Which of the following is a bad reading habit?
questions.explanation: Finger-pointing is one of the eight reading deficiencies or bad habits, along with vocalisation and regression. Previewing, annotating and reading with intent are all recommended strategies for reading efficiently.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: Regression, the habit of glancing back to re-read, is usually caused by
questions.explanation: Regression usually comes from poor concentration; some is acceptable, but too much hinders reading. A wide span of recognition is a sign of a good reader, so it does not cause regression.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: What is the correct order of the three stages of reading efficiently?

options.a: Preview before reading, review after reading, read with intent
options.b: Review before reading, read with intent, preview after reading
options.c: Preview before reading, read with intent, review after reading
options.d: Read with intent, preview before reading, review after reading

questions.explanation: You first preview the text, then read it with intent, and finally review it after reading. Putting reading with intent first skips the preview stage, where skimming and connecting to your experience take place.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: Highlighting key points and annotating your impressions belong to which stage of reading efficiently?
questions.explanation: When reading with intent you search for key elements, highlight key points and annotate your impressions. Reviewing after reading then focuses on the highlights and annotations already made, rather than creating them.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: When reading with intent, the author's main point is usually found in the
questions.explanation: The author's main point is usually stated in the thesis statement in the first or second paragraph, though it may only be implied. The conclusion is a separate key element that closes the text rather than stating the main point first.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: Personal comments that a reader writes in the margin of a text are called
questions.explanation: Annotation means writing your own comments in the margin, such as important points, questions and inconsistencies. Highlighting only marks words already in the text and adds nothing of your own.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: A diagram that shows the structure of the main points of a text, especially useful when the text is difficult, is a
questions.explanation: A graphic organiser is a diagram of how the main points fit together, and it helps with difficult texts. A table of contents lists chapters or sections; it does not map how the ideas relate.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: When highlighting a text, which practice is recommended?

options.a: Highlight every sentence that has a date
options.d: Highlight as much of the text as possible

questions.explanation: The rules are to decide what to highlight, read first and then highlight, be selective, and highlight the thesis and topic sentences. Highlighting as much as possible breaks the rule of being selective.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: When should a reader review a text after reading it?

options.a: Only if the text was difficult
options.b: Only on the eve of the examination

questions.explanation: Review after reading should be done immediately, using the same steps as previewing. Waiting until the eve of an examination means the details will already have faded.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: In reading, the eyes do the physical task. Which organ interprets what is read?
questions.explanation: Reading uses the eyes for the physical task of seeing the symbols and the brain for interpreting them. The eyes only take in the printed symbols; they do not work out the meaning.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: Which of the following statements about reading as a skill is correct?

options.a: It is fully mastered by the end of primary school
options.b: It depends only on the eyes
options.d: It is a developmental process that is never fully mastered

questions.explanation: Reading keeps developing throughout life and is never fully mastered, and its efficiency improves only with practice. It also uses the brain for interpretation, so 'only the eyes' is wrong.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a step in previewing a text?

options.a: Checking the title, subtitles and author
options.b: Reading the introduction or first paragraph
options.c: Writing a summary from your highlights and annotations
options.d: Examining photos, charts, tables and diagrams

questions.explanation: Writing a summary from highlights and annotations is part of reviewing after reading, not previewing. Checking the title and author, reading the introduction and examining charts are all among the seven previewing steps.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: Which of the following is a way of connecting a text to your own experience before reading?

options.a: Thinking of similar situations you have experienced
options.d: Copying the first paragraph word for word

questions.explanation: Connecting to your experience involves thinking of similar situations, asking and answering questions, and writing down ideas as they come. Reading only the conclusion is not a way of connecting to experience and skips most of the text.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: A trader in Balogun market glances quickly over a newspaper just to get a general idea of what it is about. Which type of reading is this?
questions.explanation: Skimming is a quick look to get the overall or general idea of a text. Scanning is also quick, but it looks for one specific piece of information, which the trader is not doing.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: Which type of reading is intensive, thorough and critical?
questions.explanation: Study reading is the intensive, thorough and critical type of reading used for serious learning. Skimming and scanning are quick runs through a text for the general idea or a specific detail.

questions.topic: Reading Skills I: Effective Reading Strategies
questions.question: In the study-reading mnemonic LEARNER, the first 'E' stands for
questions.explanation: In LEARNER, L is lay out the purpose and the first E is examine all parts. 'Ease away from one subject before starting another' is the second E, near the end of the mnemonic.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT true about writing a summary?

options.a: expressions are paraphrased with new words
options.c: quotations from the text are included

questions.explanation: A good summary paraphrases the original in new words, presents the major facts and uses the present tense, so A, B and D are all true. Including quotations from the text (option C) goes against the rule of restating ideas in your own words, so C is the statement that is not true.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: Below are the steps involved in summarising a text; arrange them in the appropriate order. i. Express the contents of the text in your own words. ii. Read to find the basic ideas iii. Compare your summary with the original text. iv. Read to find the essentials.
questions.explanation: To summarise a text, you read to find the basic idea, read again to pick out the essentials, express the content in your own words, and finally compare your summary with the original, which is the order ii, iv, i, iii. Options A and C begin with writing the summary before reading, and B begins with the comparison, which can only come last.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: A passage written in a technical or difficult language is best read ------------------
questions.explanation: Reading speed should match the difficulty of the passage, so a passage in technical or difficult language should be read at a slow pace to take in the unusual vocabulary. Option A (a fast pace) and D (skimming it once) would only give a rough idea and hurt understanding, and C is wrong because any reader can handle such a passage by slowing down.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: A comprehension passage is best understood when it is read -----------------
questions.explanation: A comprehension passage is best understood when you read it more than once, with a quick first reading for the general idea and a slower second reading for details. Options B and D fix a specific number, but the advice is not limited to two or three readings, and C (once) goes against the advice completely.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: A/an ............ is a condensed version of an original work.
questions.explanation: A summary (also called a recap) is a condensed version of an original work, usually about one-third of its length. Option C, an appendix, adds extra material at the end of a work rather than shortening it, and A (preface) and B (blurb) are front-matter and back-cover texts, not condensed versions of the work.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: In relation to the tools used by examiners to test the candidates' understanding, the following question types can be identified except ....
questions.explanation: Comprehension questions fall into four categories based on the tools examiners use: direct reference, inference, supposition and evaluation questions. There is no affirmation question among them, so C is the exception, and A, B and D are genuine types.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: The first step in reading a passage is to ------------------ it.
questions.explanation: Previewing comes first: you skim the title, headings and opening lines to get an idea of what the passage contains before reading it properly. Summarising (C) only comes after you have read, and editing and appreciating (B and A) are not stages of studying a passage.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: A/an ---------------- is a summary of a plot.
questions.explanation: A synopsis is a summary of a plot, the kind of account you give when someone asks what a film or novel was about. Storyline (D) is the plot itself rather than a summary of it, and prologue and episode (A and C) are parts of a work, not condensed versions of it.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: Questions which require you to refer directly to the text are called ....
questions.explanation: Direct reference questions are those that require you to refer directly to the text, for example asking what the passage says about a topic (C).
