Inference questions (B) ask you to work out relationships between parts of the passage, supposition questions (A) take you beyond the passage, and evaluation questions (D) ask you to judge the writer's language and information.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: When previewing a passage titled 'The Causes of Election Violence', a good strategy is to

options.a: memorise the title word for word
options.b: skip the title and read the conclusion
options.c: turn the title into a question
options.d: count the paragraphs in the passage

questions.explanation: Turning the title into a question, such as 'What are the causes of election violence?', gives your reading a purpose from the start. Skipping the title throws away the first clue to what the passage is about.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: The first reading of a comprehension passage should be

options.b: word by word, to check every meaning
options.c: rapid, to get a general impression
options.d: slow, to separate main ideas from minor ones

questions.explanation: The first reading is a quick one that gives a general impression of the tone, purpose and theme. Slow reading to separate main from minor ideas is the job of the second reading.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: Separating main ideas from minor ones, and subjective statements from objective ones, is the focus of the
questions.explanation: The second reading is slower and is used to separate main from minor ideas, subjective from objective and direct from indirect statements. The first reading is rapid and only gives a general impression.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: Which of the following is a focus of the FIRST reading of a comprehension passage?

options.a: Separating main ideas from minor ones

questions.explanation: During the first, rapid reading you look for the writer's tone and attitude, purpose and central idea. The separating tasks, such as subjective versus objective, belong to the slower second reading.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: Comprehension questions that require you to give answers in your own words are called
questions.explanation: The two major formats are multiple choice questions and traditional type questions, and the traditional type expects answers in your own words. Multiple choice questions give you options to pick from instead.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: Which of the following is a useful clue for answering comprehension multiple choice questions?

options.a: Choose the first option that seems partly correct
options.c: Use elimination to rule out wrong options

questions.explanation: Using elimination is one of the four MCQ clues, alongside making sure all other options are wrong. Choosing an option that is only partly correct is a trap, because some options are designed to be partly right.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: In comprehension MCQs, options such as 'none of the above' and 'don't know' are referred to as
questions.explanation: Options like 'none of the above' or 'don't know' are called zero answers. Partial answers are different: they are options that are only partly correct.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: A traditional comprehension question asks whether 'cat' in a passage refers to the animal or is used as a metaphor. This question tests

options.b: the meaning of a word in context

questions.explanation: Asking whether 'cat' is literal or metaphorical tests the meaning of a word in its context. It is not an opinion question, because the answer must come from how the word is used in the passage.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: Comprehension questions that require you to establish relationships between parts of the text are
questions.explanation: Inference questions ask you to connect parts of the text and see how they relate. Direct reference questions only ask you to point to what the text states.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: Comprehension questions that require you to think beyond the passage to the outside world are
questions.explanation: Supposition questions take you beyond the passage into the outside world. Inference questions stay within the text, linking one part of it to another.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: Comprehension questions that require you to judge the information and the effectiveness of the writer's language are
questions.explanation: Evaluation questions ask you to judge both the information and how well the writer uses language. Supposition questions ask you to think beyond the passage, not to judge the writer's language.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: Which of the following is an evaluation question on a comprehension passage?

options.a: How effective is the writer's use of imagery in the last paragraph?
options.b: How is the flood in paragraph 1 related to the food shortage in paragraph 3?
options.c: In what year was the bridge built, according to the passage?
options.d: What might happen in your own town if the same policy were adopted?

questions.explanation: Judging how effective the writer's imagery is assesses the writer's language, which is what evaluation questions do. Linking the flood in paragraph 1 to the food shortage in paragraph 3 is an inference question, because it connects parts of the text.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: A comprehension question asks: 'How is the drought described in paragraph 1 related to the rise in food prices in paragraph 4?' This is
questions.explanation: The question asks you to establish a relationship between two parts of the text, which makes it an inference question. A direct reference question would only ask for something stated in one place in the text.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: How many categories of comprehension question do examiners use to test understanding?
questions.explanation: There are four categories: direct reference, inference, supposition and evaluation. The figure 2 is the number of question formats (MCQ and traditional type), not categories.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: A summary is usually about what fraction of the length of the original work?
questions.explanation: A summary condenses the original to about one-third of its length. One-half would keep too much of the original to count as a proper condensed version.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: For which of the following would a synopsis, rather than a summary, be appropriate?
questions.explanation: A synopsis summarises a plot, so it is used only for novels, plays and stories. A research report has no plot, so it gets an ordinary summary.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: Short, concise summaries of non-fiction works are called
questions.explanation: Short, concise non-fiction summaries are known as abstracts. A synopsis is a plot summary used only for novels, plays and stories, so it does not fit non-fiction.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: The lead of a written summary should give

options.a: the title, author, text type and main idea
options.b: the summariser's opinion of the text
options.c: a direct quotation from the text
options.d: the dramatic climax of the text

questions.explanation: A written summary begins with a lead stating the title, the author, the type of text and its main idea. A direct quotation is out of place because a summary should not quote from the text.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: Which tense is preferred when writing a summary?

options.b: The present tense or the historic present

questions.explanation: Summaries are best written in the present tense or the historic present. The past tense is allowed for poems, stories and novels, but no past form is the preferred choice.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: Concerning tense, what should a writer AVOID in a summary?

options.a: Using the present tense for a play
options.b: Using the present tense for a novel
options.d: Shifting from one tense to another

questions.explanation: Whatever tense you choose, you should keep to it and not shift tenses. Using the present tense for a play is not a fault, because drama is summarised in the present tense.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: When summarising a multi-section document such as a report, each section should have at least how many summarising statements?
questions.explanation: For a multi-section summary, at least three summarising statements are written for each section. One statement per section is closer to a paragraph summary and would leave out too much.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: A summary strategy that integrates the ideas of a section made up of several paragraphs is a
questions.explanation: A section summary pulls together the ideas of a multi-paragraph section. A paragraph summary deals with only one paragraph at a time.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: In the third step of summarising a paragraph, the writer should

options.a: write the content in new words without looking at the original
options.b: read again to pick out the essentials
options.c: compare the summary with the original and revise it
options.d: read to find the basic idea

questions.explanation: The third step is to write the content in your own words without looking at the original. Comparing with the original and revising is the fourth and final step.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: What is the FINAL step in summarising a paragraph?

options.a: Compare your summary with the original and revise it
options.b: Express the content in your own words
options.c: Read the paragraph to find the basic idea
options.d: Read again to pick out the essentials

questions.explanation: The last of the four steps is to compare your version with the original and revise it. Expressing the content in your own words comes just before this, as the third step.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: When summarising, three or four paragraphs of an original text can be reduced to
questions.explanation: In summarising, a paragraph can become one sentence, and three or four paragraphs can become one paragraph. Keeping three paragraphs would hardly condense the text at all.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: A summary of a non-fiction work should present

options.a: the summariser's own critique of the author
options.b: a dramatic structure that builds suspense
options.c: the author's point of view without the summariser's own analysis

questions.explanation: A non-fiction summary gives the author's point of view and leaves out the summariser's own analysis. Adding your own critique turns the summary into a review.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: When summarising a book or a dissertation, the summary should use
questions.explanation: For books and dissertations, a summary should use common scientific language. Copying the writer's own exact sentences breaks the rule of paraphrasing rather than quoting.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: In Barbara Tuchman's 'A Distant Mirror', used as an illustrative text on summary, the English ordinance of 1349 was reissued in 1351 as the
questions.explanation: The extract describes the English ordinance of 1349 being reissued in 1351 as the Statute of Labourers. The Magna Carta, Poor Law and Bill of Rights are other English laws that are not connected with this extract.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: When answering a comprehension multiple choice question, how many options should a candidate mark?

options.a: Every option that is partly correct
options.c: None, if the answer is not obvious
options.d: Two, to be on the safe side

questions.explanation: Never mark more than one answer, since there is usually one correct answer. Marking every option that is partly correct is a trap, because some options are designed to be only partly right.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: The extract from T. H. Huxley's 'Collected Essays', used as an illustrative text on summary, discusses

options.a: the plague and wages in Europe
options.b: the first landing on the moon

questions.explanation: Huxley's essay deals with the distinction between 'pure' and 'applied' science. The plague and wages are the subject of the Tuchman extract, a different illustrative text.

questions.topic: Reading Skills II: Comprehension and Summary
questions.question: What should a writer do with the ideas of the original text when writing a summary?

options.a: Add a personal judgement of the author
options.c: Present them in a dramatic structure
options.d: Arrange them clearly and paraphrase them in new words

questions.explanation: A written summary arranges the ideas clearly and paraphrases them in new words. Building a dramatic structure is wrong, because a summary should have no dramatic structure.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: Prescribed text usually

options.a: Contain all the topics to be treated in a subject
options.c: Direct the reader to supplementary texts
options.d: Contain most of the topics to be treated or the basis for discussion in the lectures

questions.explanation: A prescribed text is the recommended main book for a course, and it usually contains most of the topics to be treated or forms the basis for discussion in lectures, so D is correct. Option A is too strong because no single text covers every topic, and B is wrong because lecturers use many sources. Directing readers to supplementary texts (C) is a minor side role, not its main purpose.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: Which one of these is not recommended for efficient studying

options.b: Generation of guide questions as you read

questions.explanation: Reading with pre-conceived ideas (option A) is not recommended because prejudices and emotional attachment to a subject get in the way of understanding; a good reader keeps an open, questioning mind. The other options are good study practices: asking guide questions as you read (B), varying your reading speed to suit purpose and difficulty (C), and using memory aids like mnemonics (D).

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: Supplementary texts are usually given so that

options.a: Students may have a wide reading list
options.b: Students can have the opportunity to acquire additional information for their courses
options.c: Students can fully understand the topics treated in their course
options.d: Students educational experience may be balanced

questions.explanation: Supplementary texts are given so that students can get additional information beyond what the main text covers, which is option B. The word 'supplement' means to add to. A long reading list (A) is not a goal in itself, and full understanding (C) or a balanced education (D) are too vague to be the stated purpose.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: During the reading process the saccadic and regressive eye movements are
questions.explanation: When we read, our eyes move forward in little jumps and stops along the line (saccadic movement) and sometimes move back to words already read (regressive movement). Both are part of how the eyes naturally work in reading, so D, natural reading technique, is correct. They become a problem only when regression is excessive, so A and C are too negative, and B, complementary, is not the term used for these movements.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: Your mental posture while reading is not affected by ...............

options.a: music from the radio or other gadgets
options.c: the arrangement of keywords and topic sentences

questions.explanation: Your mental posture for reading is disturbed by things like music from a radio or phone, noise, and worries about money, love or health. The arrangement of keywords and topic sentences is different: it is a reading strategy that helps you follow the text, so it does not disturb you, and C is the answer. A, B and D are all distractions.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: ---------------- is not associated with sensory memory.
questions.explanation: Sensory memory is tied to the senses, so the organs involved are the ears, eyes, hands, tongue and nose. The brain is not a sense organ; it processes information after the senses have received it, so B is the one not associated with sensory memory. A, C and D are all sense organs.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: Which of the following is not a mark of a serious student?

options.a: reading at a specific time and place

questions.explanation: A serious student plans study for a specific time at a regular place, draws up a reading timetable and avoids distractions, because a textbook, unlike a newspaper, needs a quiet, private area for understanding. Reading study materials just anywhere contradicts this, so B is not a mark of a serious student, while A, C and D are all good habits.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: 3R stands for -----------------
questions.explanation: The 3Rs in the SQ3R technique (Survey, Question, Read, Recall, Review) are Read, Recall and Review. Options A and D include steps such as Roll, Replay and Reharsh that are not part of the method. Option B is the closest trap because Recite is another name for Recall, but Repeat is not the third R.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: Which of the following is true?

options.d: We read for knowledge acquisition only

questions.explanation: People read for many different purposes, from pleasure to serious ones like examinations and acquiring knowledge. Options A, C and D each use the word only, which makes each one false, so B (none of the above) is the only correct choice.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: Reading for the purpose of gathering information that will translate to knowledge is also known as ---------------------
questions.explanation: Study reading is the type of reading we do to gather information that will turn into knowledge in a specific area, so A is correct. Scanning and skimming (C and D) are quick reading techniques for finding specific facts or getting a general idea, not for deep learning. Exploring (B) is not a reading type.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: One of the following is NOT true.

options.a: through reading, you improve upon your listening skills
options.b: through reading, you diminish your speech ability
options.c: through reading, you enlarge your vocabulary
options.d: through reading, you improve your writing skills

questions.explanation: Reading builds your ability to speak rather than weakening it, so B is the false statement. Through reading you enlarge your vocabulary, which in turn improves your listening and writing, and the extra words and structures you meet also feed your speech. Options A, C and D are all real benefits of reading.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: One of the following is a reading technique.
questions.explanation: PQRST is a method of study reading, standing for Preview, Question, Read, Summary and Test, so C is correct. Options A, B and D just scramble the letters and do not match any study technique taught in this course.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: Recalling stored information is enhanced by the following except ---------
questions.explanation: Recalling stored information is helped by repetition, recitation and review, which are all active ways of strengthening memory. Reproduction is just producing the information, for example in an exam, and does not improve recall, so B is the odd one out.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: A survey of an article or chapter in a book does not take -------------------- into consideration.
questions.explanation: Surveying an article or chapter means checking the title, the first and concluding paragraphs and the topic sentences of each paragraph. The blurb is used when surveying a whole book, since only books carry one, so A is the exception. Options B, C and D are all parts of surveying an article or chapter.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: How a reading material is read is determined by --------------------.
questions.explanation: The nature of a reading material decides how it is read and how rigorously: a newspaper is read once and discarded, while a study book is studied repeatedly (A). Option D, the reader, is tempting because readers vary their speed, but it is the material's nature that determines the approach. The author (C) and publishers (B) have no say in how you read.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: Survey, in reading, involves ---------------.

options.a: investigating the depth of the content
options.c: examining the preliminary matters and blurb of the book
options.d: measuring the length and breadth of the book

questions.explanation: In the survey stage of SQ3R, you examine the preliminary matters of a book, such as the title, preface, foreword and table of contents, and read the blurb for a summary of the book (C). Option A describes deeper study reading, not a survey, and B and D play on the everyday meaning of survey and have nothing to do with reading.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: Based on the length of storage of information, memory is classified into ------
questions.explanation: By how long information is kept, memory is divided into short-term memory, which stores information briefly and filters out what is irrelevant, and long-term memory, which is permanent and large (C). Sensory memory is the very brief memory linked to the senses. Active and dormant (D) describe kinds of vocabulary, not memory, and A and B are not memory types at all.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: The movement of the eyes in the process of reading can be described as ------------
questions.explanation: When we read, our eyes move in little jumps forward and then stop, and this movement is called saccadic (C). Velaric, glottalic and pulmonic (A, B and D) are airstream mechanisms in speech production and have nothing to do with eye movement.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: SQ3R, a method of study reading, stands for
questions.explanation: SQ3R is Survey, Question, Read, Recall/Recite and Review. Reflect and Recollect belong to the 3S3R method, not to SQ3R.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: What do the letters of the study-reading method PQRST stand for?
questions.explanation: PQRST is Preview, Question, Read, Summary and Test. The other expansions swap in words such as Recall, Study or Review, which do not belong to PQRST.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: In the OK4R method of study reading, the letter 'K' stands for
questions.explanation: OK4R is Overview, Key points, then Read, Recall, Reflect and Review. 'Key questions' sounds close, but questioning is a step in SQ3R and PQRST, not the K of OK4R.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: Which method of study reading consists of Survey, Study-read, Speech-read, Recite, Reflect and Recollect?
questions.explanation: The three S steps (Survey, Study-read, Speech-read) and three R steps (Recite, Reflect, Recollect) make up 3S3R. SQ3R also starts with Survey, but its other steps are Question, Read, Recall/Recite and Review.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: Which method of study reading gives priority to information needed for examinations?
questions.explanation: PQRST, which ends with Summary and Test, gives priority to information needed for exams. SQ3R is a general study-reading method that ends with Review rather than a test.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: The type of memory that stores information for a short time, organises it and filters out what is irrelevant is
questions.explanation: Short-term memory holds information briefly, organises it and removes what is irrelevant. Long-term memory, by contrast, is permanent and limitless.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: Which type of memory is described as permanent, large and limitless?
questions.explanation: Long-term memory is permanent, large and limitless. Short-term memory keeps information only for a short time before filtering it.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: The type of memory linked to the senses, such as the eyes, ears and tongue, and which is very ephemeral, is
questions.explanation: Sensory memory is tied to the senses and fades almost at once, which is what 'very ephemeral' means. Short-term memory lasts a little longer and organises information.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: What is the correct order of the stages of storing information in memory?
questions.explanation: Information is first encoded (read, organised and internalised), then stored (retained), and finally retrieved (recalled). Storage cannot come before encoding, because information must be taken in before it can be kept.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: Reading, organising and internalising information belong to which stage of storing information?
questions.explanation: Encoding is the stage where you read, organise and internalise information. Storage is the next stage, where the information is retained.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: The stage of storing information in which a student recalls what was learnt, aided by attention, is
questions.explanation: Retrieval is the recall stage, and attention helps it. Storage is only the keeping of information, not bringing it back out.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: Which of the following is described as the best way to remember what you read?
questions.explanation: Paraphrasing, putting ideas into your own words, is the best way to remember. Verbatim recitation suits only special cases such as play lines, foreign languages and the sciences.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: Using 'ROYGBIV' to remember the colours of the rainbow is an example of which study aid?
questions.explanation: ROYGBIV is a mnemonic device or acronym in which each letter stands for a colour, from red to violet. A flash card is a separate study aid: a card with visual clues.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: Flash cards recommended as a study aid are usually of which paper size?
questions.explanation: Flash cards are A5 in size and carry visual clues. A4 is the standard size of a full sheet, which is larger than a flash card needs to be.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: Unlike a newspaper, which is usually read once, a course book should be read

options.d: only the night before an exam

questions.explanation: The nature of what is being read decides how it is read: a newspaper is read once, but a course book is read repeatedly and with effort. Skimming a course book would give only the general idea, not the knowledge it is meant to provide.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: Which of the following is a sub-strategy of the 'Read' stage of SQ3R?

options.a: Identify verbal and sense links such as keywords and topic sentences
options.b: Assess the work by going over all the steps again
options.c: Remember the material from memory and tell it to a friend
options.d: Examine the title, preface and table of contents

questions.explanation: Identifying verbal and sense links is one of the seven sub-strategies of the Read stage. Going over all the steps again is the Review stage, which comes last.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: In SQ3R, the stage that is the same as revision is
questions.explanation: Review means assessing your work, which is the same as revision, by going over all the steps again. Recall/Recite is about remembering from memory, not revising the whole process.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: A UNILAG student closes her course book and explains the chapter from memory to a friend in her hostel. Which stage of SQ3R is she practising?
questions.explanation: Recall/Recite means remembering from memory, by paraphrasing or using the exact words, in writing or to a friend. Review is about assessing the work by going over all the steps again.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: In study reading, asking 'Is the writer objective?' and 'Does it contradict my views?' belongs to which stage of SQ3R?
questions.explanation: These are among the example questions of the Question stage of SQ3R. The Survey stage only looks over preliminary matter such as the title, preface and table of contents.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: Reading improves a student's listening and writing mainly because it

options.a: reduces the need to attend lectures

questions.explanation: Reading enlarges your vocabulary, and a bigger vocabulary in turn improves listening and writing. Training the vocal apparatus is not what reading does; reading uses the eyes and the mental faculty.

questions.topic: Reading Skills III: Study Reading
questions.question: Reading is described as a process of communication through which
questions.explanation: Reading is a process of communication through which most formal learning takes place. Decoding spoken words describes listening, not reading.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: A very important part of a paragraph is
questions.explanation: The topic sentence is the most important part of a paragraph because it states the main idea and works as a summary of the paragraph, so B is correct. A topic outline (A) and a paragraph outline (D) are planning tools rather than parts of the paragraph, and sentence structure (C) concerns individual sentences, not the idea that organizes the paragraph.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: The .............. sentence is the most important sentence in a paragraph.
questions.explanation: The topic sentence is the most important sentence in a paragraph because it states the main idea and acts as a summary of the paragraph, so A is correct. First (D) and last (B) describe positions rather than functions, and the topic sentence can appear in different places. A concluding sentence (C) is optional, so it cannot be the most important.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: The element which makes a paragraph easily understandable to the reader is ..............
questions.explanation: Coherence, option D, is the quality that makes a paragraph easy for the reader to follow, achieved through logical and verbal bridges such as repeated key words, pronouns and transition words. Unity (A) means the paragraph keeps to a single focus, and development (C) means the topic is fully discussed. Completeness (B) is not one of the named elements of a paragraph.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: A/an ---------------- paragraph describes a series of events or a process in some sort of order.
questions.explanation: A sequence paragraph describes a series of events or a process in some order, usually time order, and it uses helper words like first, second, third and previously. Option B (explanation) tells how or why something happens, C (evaluation) makes judgements, and A (descriptive) paints a picture of a person, place or thing, so none of them is about order of events.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: ................. is not a step in paragraph development.
questions.explanation: The steps in paragraph development are: choose a controlling idea and write a topic sentence, explain the controlling idea, give an example or examples, explain the examples, and then complete the idea or lead into the next paragraph. Since A, B and D are all genuine steps, C, none of these, is the answer to a question asking which is not a step.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: One of the following is a feature shared by both paragraphs and essays:
questions.explanation: Both a good paragraph and a good essay show unity and coherence: unity means sticking to a single focus, and coherence means the ideas flow logically and are easy to follow. Options A, B and C each pair in something that is not a core feature, such as self sufficiency or transparency, or name transition, which is only a device for achieving coherence.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: It is NOT ideal to begin a new paragraph when:

options.a: readers need a pause in a long stretch of text
options.b: the next statement contrasts with the preceding information
options.c: you want to introduce a new idea
options.d: you are still developing the same main idea

questions.explanation: A paragraph keeps to a single main idea, so while you are still developing that idea you should stay in the same paragraph, which makes D correct. A new paragraph is the right move when you introduce a new idea (C), when the next statement contrasts with what came before (B), or when readers need a pause (A).

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: A/an ---------------- paragraph explains how or why something happens.
questions.explanation: An explanation paragraph explains how or why something happens, exploring causes and effects with helper words like because, therefore and thus. Option A (definition) explains key words, C (choice) states a preference, and D (sequence) describes events in time order.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT true of paragraphs?

options.a: every paragraph begins with a topic sentence
options.c: a paragraph is hardly ever longer than the entire essay.
options.d: the argument in a paragraph addresses only an aspect of the topic

questions.explanation: The topic sentence is often but not always the first sentence of a paragraph: it can come in the middle or at the end, and sometimes the main idea is so obvious that none is stated. So it is not true that every paragraph begins with one, and A is correct. Options B, C and D (varying lengths, shorter than the whole essay, addressing one aspect of the topic) are all true of paragraphs.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: We need to troubleshoot a paragraph in all the following cases except ..............

options.a: when it is too long or too short
options.b: when there is a problem with its topic sentence
options.c: when it has multiple controlling ideas
options.d: when it has issues with transition within the paragraph

questions.explanation: A paragraph needs troubleshooting when its topic sentence is faulty, when it has multiple controlling ideas, or when its transitions are weak. Length alone is not a fault, because length does not decide what makes a paragraph, so A is the exception. Options B, C and D are all real reasons to troubleshoot.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: One of the following is NOT a way of enhancing coherence.
questions.explanation: Pronouns that refer back to nouns in earlier sentences help build coherence, so avoiding pronouns does not enhance it; it only makes writing clumsy and repetitive (D). Repeating keywords, using synonyms and using transition words (A, B and C) are all genuine ways of creating verbal bridges between sentences.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: A/an -------------- is a unit of any composition comprising a collection of related sentences dealing with a single topic.
questions.explanation: A paragraph is a unit of composition made up of related sentences dealing with a single topic, so D is correct. An essay (C) is bigger, because it combines ideas from one paragraph to another. A sentence (A) is smaller than the unit described, and a text (B) is too general.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: The ............... in a paragraph states the main idea in that paragraph and works as its summary.
questions.explanation: The topic sentence states the main idea of a paragraph and works as its summary (D). Option B, conclusion, is wrong because the concluding sentence only closes the paragraph and is optional. A sentence in general (A) need not carry the main idea, and punctuation (C) is not a sentence at all.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: A paragraph is complete when it has ..............

options.a: an initial capital letter and a a final full stop
options.c: a topic sentence and supporting details

questions.explanation: A paragraph has a topic sentence (essential), supporting or detail sentences (essential) and a concluding sentence (optional), so it is complete once it has a topic sentence with supporting details (C). Option A describes the mechanics of a sentence, not a paragraph, and D is wrong because not every paragraph argues a point.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: To develop a paragraph, a .............. step process is advised.
questions.explanation: Paragraph development follows a 5-step process: decide on a controlling idea and write a topic sentence, explain it, give examples, explain the examples, and complete the idea or move on to the next paragraph. So B is correct, and 1, 7 and 3 (A, C and D) give the wrong number of steps.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: Unity in a paragraph suggests ........
questions.explanation: Unity means the whole paragraph keeps a single focus and does not wander into different ideas, so B is correct. Connection with other paragraphs (A) is about linking paragraphs with transitions, not about unity within one paragraph. Brevity (D) is about length, and elocution (C) concerns speaking.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: A/an .... is a combination of ideas from one paragraph to another, that creates a united whole.
questions.explanation: An essay is a combination of ideas from one paragraph to another that creates a united whole, because all the paragraphs support each other (B). A paragraph (D) is the single unit being combined, not the combination itself, a sentence (C) is smaller still, and a text (A) is too general.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: To develop a paragraph properly, a writer should normally write at least
questions.explanation: A paragraph should have at least three sentences; single-sentence paragraphs are rare. Two sentences is too few, since paragraphs of only two or three sentences risk inadequate development.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: A paragraph that uses expressions such as 'can be divided into', 'falls under' and 'belongs to' is a
questions.explanation: These expressions group things into categories, which is what a classification paragraph does. A definition paragraph instead explains key words with phrases such as 'is defined as'.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: A paragraph that uses words such as 'on the other hand', 'in contrast to' and 'differs from' is a
questions.explanation: These words show similarities and differences, the work of a comparison and contrast paragraph. A classification paragraph groups things into categories rather than setting them against each other.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: A paragraph that judges people, ideas or actions against criteria and uses words such as 'suggest', 'recommend' and 'advise' is a/an
questions.explanation: An evaluation paragraph judges against criteria (good or bad, correct or incorrect) and makes recommendations. A choice paragraph only states a personal preference without judging against criteria.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: A paragraph in an economics essay begins: 'Inflation is defined as a sustained rise in the general price level.' What type of paragraph is it most likely to be?
questions.explanation: The helper phrase 'is defined as' marks a definition paragraph, which explains key words. A classification paragraph would use phrases such as 'can be divided into' to group things.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: A paragraph that uses words of measurement, location, size, colour and shape, and phrases like 'resembles', is a
questions.explanation: Words of size, colour, shape and location, and 'resembles', describe a person, place or thing, which makes a descriptive paragraph. A comparison and contrast paragraph focuses on similarities and differences between two things.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: How many types of paragraph are identified, from definition to evaluation?
questions.explanation: Eight types are identified: definition, classification, descriptive, comparison and contrast, sequence, choice, explanation and evaluation. The figure 11 is the number of methods of paragraph development, a different list.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: A topic sentence is best placed at the END of a paragraph when

options.d: specific details lead up to a generalisation

questions.explanation: When the paragraph builds from specific details towards a general point, the topic sentence goes at the end. When the main idea is obvious, the topic sentence can be left out altogether rather than moved.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: When may a writer leave out the topic sentence of a paragraph?

options.a: When the main idea is obvious
options.b: When the writer is unsure of the main idea
options.c: When the paragraph has many examples
options.d: When the paragraph is the conclusion

questions.explanation: A topic sentence can be left out when the main idea is already obvious to the reader. Being unsure of the main idea is a reason to fix the paragraph, not to drop the topic sentence.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: In a concise and emphatic topic sentence such as 'The Nigerian banking system has collapsed', the key word is placed
questions.explanation: A good topic sentence is concise and emphatic, with the key word placed at the end, as 'collapsed' is in the example. Placing it at the beginning loses the emphasis that the final position gives.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: In the structure of a paragraph, the concluding sentence is

options.a: essential, and simply repeats the topic sentence
options.b: a summary only, with no link to what follows
options.c: optional, and leads to the next step
options.d: always the first sentence of the paragraph

questions.explanation: The concluding sentence is optional and is more than a summary, because it leads to the next step. It usually comes last or second-to-last, never first.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: A body paragraph that is full of evidence but has very little analysis is weak because
questions.explanation: Evidence without analysis leaves the paragraph with no argument. An unsupported claim is the opposite problem, which happens when there is plenty of analysis but too little evidence.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: Very short paragraphs in an essay often suggest
questions.explanation: Very short paragraphs suggest a lack of substance. Poor structure is what very long paragraphs tend to suggest, so it is the tempting but wrong choice here.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: In the five-step process of paragraph development, what comes right after explaining the controlling idea?

options.d: Completing the idea or moving to the next paragraph

questions.explanation: The steps are: decide on a controlling idea, explain it, give an example, explain the example, then complete the paragraph or transition. Explaining the example is step 4, so it comes after the example has been given.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: In the five-step process of paragraph development, which steps may be repeated?

options.a: Explaining examples and completing the paragraph (steps 4 and 5)
options.b: Giving examples and explaining them (steps 3 and 4)
options.c: Explaining the controlling idea and giving examples (steps 2 and 3)
options.d: Deciding on and explaining the controlling idea (steps 1 and 2)

questions.explanation: Steps 3 and 4, giving an example and explaining it, can be repeated to develop the paragraph further. The controlling idea in steps 1 and 2 is set only once, since a paragraph should have a single focus.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: A paragraph that contains multiple controlling ideas should be fixed by

options.b: removing sentences or splitting the paragraph

questions.explanation: Multiple controlling ideas break unity, so the remedy is to remove the off-focus sentences or split the paragraph. Adding more examples would only make the paragraph longer without fixing its divided focus.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four elements of an effective paragraph?
questions.explanation: The four elements are unity, coherence, a topic sentence and adequate development. Length is not one of them; in fact paragraphs are hardly ever longer than one double-spaced page.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: Repeating keywords, using synonyms and using pronouns that refer back to nouns build coherence through
questions.explanation: Verbal bridges are word-level links: repeated keywords, synonyms, pronouns and transition words. Logical bridges work at the level of ideas, carrying the same idea from sentence to sentence or using parallel forms.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: Carrying the same idea from sentence to sentence and using parallel sentence forms build coherence through
questions.explanation: Logical bridges carry the same idea through the paragraph and use parallel sentence forms. Verbal bridges are word-based links such as repeated keywords and synonyms.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a method of paragraph development?
questions.explanation: Anecdote, testimony and chronology are among the eleven methods of developing a paragraph. Punctuation is a writing convention, not a way of developing an idea.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: Internal aids, usually several sentences or a whole paragraph, that outline what has been covered and where the text is going are called
questions.explanation: Signposts tell the reader what has been covered and what comes next. Transitions are shorter links, one or more sentences, that move from one idea to the next.

questions.topic: Writing Skills I: The Paragraph
questions.question: One or more sentences that move from one idea to the next, often at the end of a paragraph, are called
questions.explanation: Transitions move the reader from one idea to the next and often sit at the end of a paragraph. Signposts are larger aids that outline what has been covered and where the text is going.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: A full essay must have 3 main features

options.a: Appropriate choice of words & acceptable sentences
options.c: Coherence & use of standard writing conventions

questions.explanation: Option D, all of the above, is correct because each of A, B and C names a real feature of a full essay: appropriate word choice and acceptable sentences, good paragraphing and grammatical sentences, and coherence with standard writing conventions. Choosing just one of A, B or C would leave out features that are equally required in a complete essay.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: Major features of any good writing include;
questions.explanation: Any good piece of writing, like a good lecture or essay, moves from an introduction through a middle (the main body) to a conclusion, so B is correct. Option A wrongly puts the summary in the middle, and C leaves out the conclusion, so neither gives the standard three-part structure.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: In report writing, the situation must be based on
questions.explanation: A report presents a situation to readers who may have to act on it, so it must be based on facts, which is option D. Hearsay (A) is unverified talk and has no place in a report, and arguments (B) belong to persuasive writing. Proof (C) is close, but proof is what you use to support a claim; the report itself rests on the facts of the situation observed.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: The narrative essay has all but one of the following feature
questions.explanation: A strong argument (option D) is the feature a narrative essay does not need. A narrative essay is a sequential or chronological account of an experience or incident, marked by suspense and other devices so the reader feels a good story has been told. Suspense (A), story line (B) and plot (C) are all narrative features, while a strong argument belongs to the argumentative or persuasive essay.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: A thesis statement is to an essay what a topic sentence is to;
questions.explanation: A topic sentence states the main idea of its paragraph, just as a thesis statement states the central idea of the whole essay, so the parallel is with the paragraph, option C. The topic sentence works as the thesis of the paragraph. Options A, B and D are wrong because every paragraph has a topic sentence that controls it, not just the introductory, concluding or main one.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: A police statement is an example of;
questions.explanation: A police statement recounts what happened step by step, in the order events occurred, so it is narrative writing, option C. Narrative writing is a sequential or chronological account of an experience, procedure or incident, and it is largely reportorial in nature. It is not academic writing (A) or a research report (D), and although it reports facts, it is not a technical report (B) because it does not deal with specialized technical procedures.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: The main features of an introductory paragraph are;

options.a: Statement of thesis, setting of tone, plan
options.b: Quotation, topic sentence, summary of essay

questions.explanation: An introductory paragraph states the thesis, sets the tone and gives the reader a plan of what will follow, so A is correct. A good introduction also arouses the reader's interest and keeps attention on the central theme. Options B and C include a summary of the essay, which belongs in the conclusion, not the introduction.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: Mechanics of writing consists of;
questions.explanation: Mechanics of writing means the symbols and conventions that organize writing on the page rather than the words themselves, and that covers punctuation, capitalization, and spelling and letter shapes. Since A, B and C are each part of mechanics, D, all of the above, is correct. Choosing only one would leave out other parts of mechanics.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: One of these is a punctuation mark used in dialogue after a speakers name
questions.explanation: In written dialogue, a colon follows the speaker's name to introduce the words spoken, as in Okon said: I am hungry, so D is correct. A full stop (A) would end the sentence before the speech begins, a semi-colon (B) joins related clauses, and option C, University, is not a punctuation mark at all.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: The ____ is used to mark off initials
questions.explanation: The full stop, option B, marks off initials and abbreviations, as in E. A. Adedun, Mr., Prof. or Ph.D. A semi-colon (A) joins clauses, a bracket (C) encloses extra material and a dash (D) sets off interrupting material, so none of them is used for initials.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: One of the following punctuation marks is used in pairs
questions.explanation: Quotation marks, option D, always come in pairs: one to open the quoted words and one to close them, enclosing someone's exact words. A question mark (A), hyphen (B) and apostrophe (C) are each used singly, so they do not fit the description.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: Brackets are used to enclose
questions.explanation: Brackets enclose material that is additional to the main statement, and a typical example in academic writing is a reference, such as the author and year placed in brackets after a quotation, so A is correct. Main ideas (B) are never bracketed because they must stand out, and book titles (C) are shown in italics or underlined, which also makes D wrong.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: Exclamation marks are used for
questions.explanation: The exclamation mark is used at the end of a structure expressing surprise, horror, excitement or any strong feeling, and it punctuates interjections such as ouch, hey and oh, so B is correct. Listings (A) are introduced by a colon, and confessions (C) and music (D) have no special link to the exclamation mark.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: One of the following is used to introduce additional information
questions.explanation: The dash, option C, introduces or sets off additional information that interrupts the main statement, as in All managers - I mean most managers - look forward to vacations. A full stop (A) ends a sentence, an apostrophe (B) shows possession or omission, and a hyphen (D) joins parts of words, so none of these introduces extra information.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: Capitalization is necessary in all but one of the following

options.d: Names of deities and sacred contexts

questions.explanation: Capital letters are needed at the start of a sentence, for the pronoun I, and for proper nouns, including names of deities and sacred contexts. Common nouns (option B) such as table or city are written in lower case unless they begin a sentence, so B is the one case where capitalization is not necessary.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: Which of the following is used to indicate possession in English?
questions.explanation: The apostrophe, option C, shows possession in English, as in Ade's salary or Moses' allowance. Inverted commas (A) and quotation marks (D) are the same thing and enclose quoted speech, while a hyphen (B) joins parts of compound words.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: The punctuation mark used for interrogative sentence is ____
questions.explanation: An interrogative sentence asks a question, and a direct question ends with a question mark, so C is correct. The exclamation mark (A) marks strong feeling, the period or full stop (B) ends a statement or command, and the colon (D) introduces a list or quotation.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: Another name for the period is ___
questions.explanation: Period is simply the American name for the full stop, so C is correct; it ends declarative and imperative sentences. The semi-colon (A), hyphen (B) and exclamation mark (D) are different marks with different uses, so they are not other names for the period.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: Brainstorming is one of the fundamentals of ____
questions.explanation: Brainstorming means freely generating and jotting down ideas on a topic before organizing them, and it is a fundamental first step in writing a good essay, so A is correct. It belongs to the planning stage, when the writer gathers material and decides on a central idea. It is not a way of passing examinations in general (B), and it works on ideas for a whole piece rather than a single sentence (C) or improving an already written paragraph (D).

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: To ensure that the different paragraphs of an essay are properly related, you must use
questions.explanation: To make the paragraphs of an essay flow into one another, you use linking expressions, option C, such as first, second, finally, furthermore, in addition and however. They show continuity with the idea already expressed. Lexical equivalence (A) and descriptive expressions (D) are not connecting devices, and introductory remarks (B) only open the essay rather than tie paragraphs together.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: To mark off two or more independent clauses in a sentence, you should use a ___
questions.explanation: A semi-colon, option B, marks off two or more independent clauses in one sentence, replacing a comma plus a coordinating conjunction, as in Supply us with three cars; they must all be black. Paired commas (A) and parentheses (D) enclose extra material inside a sentence rather than separating clauses, and emphasis (C) is not a punctuation mark.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: Which of the following is not a common essay type
questions.explanation: Essays are commonly classed as narrative, expository (analytical), argumentative (persuasive) or descriptive, so A, B and C are all common essay types. A proposal (option D) is a business or research document that puts forward a plan, not a type of essay, so it is the answer to this 'is not' question.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: A faithful account of an activity in which the writer participated can be labeled
questions.explanation: A faithful, factual account of an activity in which the writer took part is a report, option A, because a report records what actually happened for others to read and act on. A memo (B) is a short internal message, prolegomena (C) means a preliminary introduction to a book, and an episode (D) is a single event in a story rather than an account of one.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: A high degree of objectivity is normally expected in
questions.explanation: Scientific writing, option A, demands the highest degree of objectivity because it reports observations, data and results that must be verifiable whatever the writer feels. Informal writing (B) is personal by nature, and formal writing (C) is a broad category that includes opinion pieces, so formality alone does not guarantee objectivity. Doctor-patient writing (D) is not a recognized category of writing.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: Technical writing may not include
questions.explanation: Technical writing deals with factual, practical or specialized information in fields such as engineering, law and public administration, so a car manual (A), police reports (C) and law reports (D) are all technical documents. Love poems (option B) are imaginative and emotional, the opposite of technical writing, so B is what technical writing may not include.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: Which of the following is not one of the main divisions of the writing process
questions.explanation: The writing process is usually divided into a pre-writing stage (planning and gathering ideas), a writing stage (drafting) and a proof-reading stage (checking and correcting), so A, B and D are genuine divisions. Publishing (option C) is what may happen to a finished piece afterwards, not a stage of writing it, so C is the one that does not belong.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: In technical writing, the acronym SME means
questions.explanation: In technical writing, SME stands for Subject Matter Expert, option C: the specialist whose knowledge the writer draws on to make sure the content is accurate. Options A, B and D are made-up expansions that do not correspond to any recognized term in technical communication.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: Which of the following would you write under subscription in a letter
questions.explanation: The subscription of a letter is the closing formula written just before the signature, such as Yours faithfully or Yours sincerely, so B is correct. The addressee's designation (A) belongs in the inside address at the top, the salutation (C) is the opening greeting such as Dear Sir, and the body (D) is the main message of the letter.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: One of the following will provide information to influence our decisions and actions
questions.explanation: Reports, option A, are written to supply the information decision makers need in order to decide and act, for example a committee report recommending a course of action. A memorandum (B) mainly passes on brief internal messages, an agenda (C) only lists the items for a meeting, and anecdotes (D) are short entertaining stories, not a reliable basis for decisions.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: The goal of an argumentative essay is to ..............
questions.explanation: An argumentative or persuasive essay tries to get readers to accept a point of view: it sells an idea, convinces readers and persuades the audience. Since all three of the listed goals are correct, all of the above is the right answer. Choosing just one of them would give only part of what an argumentative essay sets out to do.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_is used to introduce a list
questions.explanation: The colon, option A, introduces a list, especially after words like the following or namely, as in Please purchase the following items: a suitcase, a pair of shoes and a bottle of perfume. A full stop (B) ends a sentence, a semi-colon (C) joins related clauses or separates items that already contain commas, and a comma (D) separates the items within the list rather than introducing it.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: One of the following is not a type of essay:
questions.explanation: Essays are classed by content and purpose into narrative, analytical, persuasive and descriptive types, so narrative (B), analytical (C) and descriptive (D) are all genuine essay types. Experimental, option A, describes a method of scientific inquiry, not a type of essay, so it is the answer to this 'not' question.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: Which of the following is correct?
questions.explanation: Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe, so the correct forms are theirs, yours and its. Option D, the dog wagged its tail, follows this rule. Options A and B wrongly add apostrophes to possessive pronouns, and option C uses it's, which is a contraction of it is, not the possessive.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: The "period" is also written as \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ in punctuation
questions.explanation: The mark used at the end of a complete declarative or imperative sentence is called the full stop or period; the two names refer to the same symbol, so C is correct. A colon (A) introduces lists, quotation marks (B) enclose direct speech, and a comma (D) separates items within a sentence, so none of them is another name for the period.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: A .............. essay gives a detailed and often dispassionate account of people, incidents, scenes and situations in a vivid manner.
questions.explanation: A descriptive essay gives a detailed and often dispassionate account of people, incidents, scenes and situations so the reader can picture them as if present, so D is correct. A narrative essay (A) tells events in sequence, an analytical essay (B) explains or evaluates, and a persuasive essay (C) argues for a point of view.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: The terminal punctuation includes all except one
questions.explanation: The full stop, question mark and exclamation mark are terminal punctuation marks because they signal the end of a sentence. The comma separates words, phrases and clauses inside a sentence and never ends one, so A is the odd one out. Options B, C and D are all terminal marks.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: The main function of \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ is to separate independent clause
questions.explanation: The semicolon is used to separate two independent clauses that could each stand alone, replacing a comma plus a coordinating conjunction, as in Supply us with three cars; they must all be black. So C is correct. A comma (D) is tempting, but a comma alone between independent clauses creates the error called a comma splice. A colon (B) introduces lists and an exclamation mark (A) ends excited statements.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: ................. is referred to as the meat of the essay.
questions.explanation: Content is the depth of treatment of the subject matter, and the knowledge and authority brought to the discussion, and it is described in everyday terms as the meat of the essay. So A is correct. Expression (B) is about choice of words, mechanics (C) is about punctuation and similar conventions, and organization (D) is the ordering of material; none of them is the substance itself.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: The ................. is the major point which an essay seeks to prove
questions.explanation: A good essay proves a major point, and that point is called the thesis, option A; it is the central idea and organizing principle that guides the choice of material. A theme (D) is the general subject area, subject matter (C) is what the essay is about rather than what it argues, and a synopsis (B) is a summary, for example of a plot.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: Apostrophes are used \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_
questions.explanation: Apostrophes are used for contractions, option C, to show that letters have been omitted, as in won't. They are also used to show possession, as in Ade's salary. Option D is wrong because apostrophes are never used simply to form plurals, and they are not used in possessive pronouns like theirs or its. Options A and B are not functions of any punctuation mark.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: Clear thinking, accurate data, reliable authority and clear conclusion are applicable to ........ essay.
questions.explanation: An analytical essay is built on clear thinking, accurate or verified data, reliable authority and clear conclusions drawn from the evidence, so D is correct. Option A (persuasive) leans on details plus appeals to emotion, B (narrative) tells a story in sequence, and C (descriptive) gives vivid accounts of scenes and people.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: In essay writing, the acronym COEM means ................
questions.explanation: COEM stands for Content, Organisation, Expression and Mechanics, the four quality-control components of a good essay, so B is correct. The other options each swap one word for a wrong one: A uses Entertainment instead of Expression, C uses Comment instead of Content, and D uses Orientation instead of Organisation.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: A question mark is not used at the end of ............
questions.explanation: A question mark is not used after an indirect (reported) question, because that kind of question is really a statement, as in The manager demanded to know why production was slow. So D is correct. A direct question (B), a tag question (A) such as She is here, isn't she? and an echo question (C) such as Bisi has travelled? all end with a question mark.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: ............... is the informed evaluation of imaginative writing.
questions.explanation: Criticism is the analytical way of writing that gives an informed evaluation of imaginative writing, and critiques are one strategy of the analytical essay. Option B (coherence) is a quality of a good paragraph, C (blogging) is not an academic method, and D (essay writing) is too broad to be the specific word for judging literature.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: .............. is the punctuation mark used to express all forms of excitement.
questions.explanation: The exclamation mark is used at the end of a structure expressing surprise, horror, disappointment, anger, indeed all forms of excitement, as in Look out! or Oh, boy! Option B (question mark) ends direct questions, C (semi-colon) joins closely related independent clauses, and D (colon) introduces lists.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: To achieve depth in the treatment of a topic, the writer is advised to ......
questions.explanation: Depth of content depends on size: a large subject such as population growth cannot be treated exhaustively, so a writer must limit or narrow the subject at the start. Option D (expanding the subject) does the opposite and leads to skimming the surface. A and B (punctuation, transition) belong to mechanics and organisation, not depth of content.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: Identify the incorrectly capitalised sentence

options.a: The Parthenon is a temple dedicated to the goddess Athena
options.b: The Jewish festival of Passover commemorates the Exodus from Egypt
options.c: a parsnip is a root vegetable native to Eurasia
options.d: Blaise Pascal is a French scientist and mystic

questions.explanation: Every sentence must begin with a capital letter, and option C starts with a lower-case a (a parsnip is a root vegetable native to Eurasia), so it is incorrectly capitalised. Options A, B and D all begin with capitals and correctly capitalise their proper nouns (Parthenon, Athena, Passover, Egypt, Blaise Pascal, French).

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: What punctuation mark is used to express surprise?
questions.explanation: The exclamation mark is used at the end of a structure expressing surprise, horror, disappointment or any strong feeling. Option D (question mark) marks a direct question, B (full stop) ends an ordinary statement, and A (semi colon) separates clauses.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: Which of the following should not be capitalised?
questions.explanation: Gaelic, Chilean and Guatemalan are proper adjectives taken from the names of a language and nationalities, and proper nouns and their related forms take capital letters. Guesstimates is an ordinary common noun, so C should not be capitalised unless it begins a sentence.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: Identify the sentence that is incorrectly capitalised

options.a: The nfl will repeat the best of the season this summer.
options.b: I'm going to be taking history next term.
options.c: Take a U-turn at that sign.
options.d: The PTA will fund our end-of-the-year party.

questions.explanation: Acronyms and initialisms such as UNICEF, FIFA and PTA are written in capital letters, so 'nfl' should be NFL, which makes A incorrectly capitalised. Option B is correct because ordinary school subjects such as history take a small letter, and C and D capitalise U-turn and PTA properly.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: Parentheses are used to enclose\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ within a sentence
questions.explanation: Parentheses mark off additional or explanatory information within a sentence, something the sentence still makes sense without. Option A describes square brackets, which enclose words someone else adds to a quotation. Spelling errors and slang (B and D) are not what parentheses are for.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: .............. is used to separate phrases and clauses in a series within a sentence when those items already contain commas.
questions.explanation: When items in a series already contain commas, the semicolon separates them so the reader can see where each item ends, as in a list of names and their job titles. Option B (comma) is tempting, but more commas would make such a list confusing. The colon (C) introduces a list rather than separating its items, and the hyphen (D) joins words.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: The thesis statement is to an essay what the ............... is to a paragraph.
questions.explanation: The topic sentence states the main idea of a paragraph and acts as the thesis of that paragraph, just as the thesis statement carries the central idea of a whole essay. Option A, supporting details, backs up the main idea rather than stating it. Introduction and conclusion (C and D) are parts of an essay, not the single controlling sentence of a paragraph.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: A good essay should contain .....................

options.b: a variation of long and short paragraphs

questions.explanation: A good essay mixes long and short paragraphs. Too many short paragraphs make the writing choppy, while too many long ones make it boring, so variety improves the flow of ideas (B). Options A, C and D each rely mainly on one length, which is the problem to avoid.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: One of the following is NOT necessary when writing an argument.
questions.explanation: Creating a mental picture is the aim of descriptive writing, which appeals to visual and sensory perception, so it is not needed in an argument (B). Argument or persuasive writing relies on the use of details and the appeal to emotion, which is why A and D are necessary and therefore not the answer.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: In interpreting the results of experiments, .............. is/are often explored.
questions.explanation: When interpreting the results of experiments, a combination of rationalisation, critique and empirical methods might be needed, so all three are explored and D is the complete answer. Options A, B and C each name only one of the three approaches.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: Analytical essays focus on the following except .............

options.a: providing a sequential or chronological account
options.b: assessment of the implication for human existence

questions.explanation: Giving a sequential or chronological account of events is the defining feature of a narrative essay, not an analytical one (A). An analytical essay identifies an issue, examines it in detail and assesses its implications for human existence, which is why B, C and D all belong to analysis.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: One of the following is not a linking device:
questions.explanation: Because is a subordinating conjunction that joins a dependent clause to a main clause inside one sentence, so it is not a linking device in the sense of connecting paragraphs (D). Furthermore, however and finally (A, B and C) are linking devices that show how one idea continues from the one before.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: Punctuation marks are used for the following except

options.a: to separate subordinate idea from major ones in a sentence
options.b: to indicate stretches of direct speeches in a discourse
options.d: to show possessive case in proper and common nouns

questions.explanation: Punctuation marks organise and structure writing so it conveys the right meaning: commas separate subordinate ideas from main ones, quotation marks mark direct speech, and the apostrophe shows possession in nouns.
