Nothing in punctuation reveals a writer's background, so C is the odd one out, while A, B and D are real functions of punctuation.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: The colon is used in the following situations except

options.a: to introduce a list after words such as 'the following'
options.b: to introduce direct speech in some contexts
options.c: to join the parts of a compound word such as sister-in-law
options.d: to separate a title from its subtitle

questions.explanation: Joining the parts of a compound word such as sister-in-law is the job of the hyphen, not the colon, so C is the exception. The colon introduces a list, especially after 'the following' or 'as follows' (A), can introduce direct speech, as in Okon said: "I am hungry." (B), and separates a title from its subtitle (D).

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: The __________ is used before a list of items
questions.explanation: The colon introduces a list, especially after words like 'these', 'namely', 'the following' or 'as follows' (A). The semicolon (B) separates items within a list that already contain commas, but it does not introduce the list. The period (C) ends a sentence and the question mark (D) ends a direct question.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: Another name for the argumentative essay is ........ essay.
questions.explanation: The argumentative essay is also called the persuasive essay, because the writer takes a stand and tries to get readers to accept a point of view (C). Expository (D) describes writing that explains or informs rather than argues, and authoritative and rational (A and B) are not names of essay types.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: The chief aim of a narrative essay is to ......

options.c: create a mental image of something

questions.explanation: The chief aim of a narrative essay is to arouse and sustain the reader's interest, making them feel a good story has been told (A). Defending a position (B) is the aim of argumentative writing, creating a mental image (C) belongs to the descriptive essay, and explaining a process (D) is expository or analytical.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: An analytical essay provides information such as ..............
questions.explanation: In an analytical essay, information comes in two basic forms: rationalisations, which explain the state of things, and critiques, which review and judge quality. Since A and C are both correct, 'all of the above' (B) is the right choice, and 'none of the above' (D) is plainly wrong.

questions.topic: Writing Skills II: Essay Writing and Punctuation
questions.question: The ................. essay emphasizes character and setting.
questions.explanation: A narrative essay emphasises character and setting so that the reader can identify with the subject and the situation (B). Option A, descriptive, is tempting because description also paints scenes, but character and setting are tied specifically to narration. Persuasive and analytical essays (C and D) focus on arguments and analysis.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: The dictionary contain all but information on

options.d: The year the words become obsolete

questions.explanation: A dictionary gives a word's spelling, meaning, pronunciation, usage, synonyms, etymology (origin) and grammatical functions. So meaning (A), pronunciation (B) and etymology (C) are all found there. The year a word became obsolete (option D) is not recorded; at most a dictionary labels a word as archaic, so D is the answer.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: Who ______ the telephone?
questions.explanation: Invented is correct because the telephone is a device that did not exist until someone created it. We discover things that already exist, such as a planet or a mineral, so discovered is the most tempting wrong choice. Founded is used for organisations and explored for places, so neither fits.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: The judge was ______ that the man was guilty
questions.explanation: Convinced is correct because it means made to believe that something is true, which is what happens when a judge accepts that a man is guilty. Persuaded is the tempting choice, but it is normally used for being talked into doing something (persuaded to confess), not for believing a fact. Believed and trusted cannot be used in the pattern 'was ... that' here.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: He ______ a prize for his diligence
questions.explanation: Received is correct because a prize is given to someone, so that person receives it. Took suggests he seized or helped himself to the prize, which does not fit being rewarded for diligence. Made and performed do not collocate with prize at all.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: It is not wise to ______ family quarrels
questions.explanation: We interfere in matters or affairs that are not our business, such as a family quarrel, so interfere in is correct. Interfere with is used when something disturbs, obstructs or tampers with something else, for example noise interfering with your reading. Interfere on and interfere at are not standard English.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: She did not ______ to go
questions.explanation: To agree to do something means to say yes to a proposal or request, so agree is correct. Accept is the tempting choice, but it takes a noun object, as in accept an offer, so 'she did not accept to go' is non-standard. Allow would need an object (allow him to go), and admit to means to confess, so neither fits.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: A butcher ______ meat
questions.explanation: To deal in something means to buy and sell it as a trade, so a butcher deals in meat. Deals with means to handle or manage a problem or person, which gives the wrong meaning here. Deals on and deals at are not standard expressions.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: How does that man ______ his living?
questions.explanation: We earn a living, meaning we work to get the money we need, so earn is correct. Win goes with prizes, games or competitions, so you cannot win your living. Achieve and score do not collocate with living either.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: Please ______ me to give the money back
questions.explanation: To remind someone is to make them remember something, which is exactly what the speaker wants, so remind is correct. Remember is something you do yourself, so 'please remember me to give the money back' is wrong. Recall and memorise also describe your own mental action and cannot take the pattern 'me to give'.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: The judge ______ the wrong done to the child
questions.explanation: To avenge a wrong is to punish the wrongdoer on behalf of the victim, which is what a judge does in the name of justice, so avenged is correct. Revenged carries the idea of personal retaliation, as in revenging yourself on an enemy, so it does not fit a judge acting for a child. Retaliated and rebelled cannot take 'the wrong' as a direct object.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: Some people ________ freedom so much that they are ready to die for it
questions.explanation: Love expresses a deep, intense feeling strong enough to make people willing to die for something, so it is correct. Like is far weaker, meaning only to find something pleasant, so it does not match the seriousness of being ready to die. Prefer and fancy are also too weak, and prefer needs a comparison.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: The word here that can take the suffix, -NESS, by way of spelling is;
questions.explanation: The suffix -ness turns adjectives into nouns, and apt is an adjective, so aptness, option A, is correct. Sadly (B) and happily (D) are adverbs, so they cannot take -ness in that form; the -ness words come from the adjectives sad and happy. Comfort (C) is already a noun, so comfortness is not a word.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: A basic reference tool every university student should personally own for effective study is ___
questions.explanation: A good dictionary, option A, is the most basic tool a student needs, because it gives the meaning, spelling, pronunciation and usage of words needed in every course, and helps you grow your vocabulary. A well equipped library (B) and an encyclopedia (C) are valuable resources, but they are not the personal basic tool every student must own, so D is also wrong.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: Poetic meaning of an expression is usually
questions.explanation: Poetic meaning is usually figurative, option C, because poets use words beyond their literal dictionary sense to suggest images, feelings and associations. Denotative meaning (B) is the literal meaning, which is the opposite of what poetry relies on, and expressive (A) and discursive (D) are not the standard terms for this kind of meaning.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: Denotative words are

options.a: Words which refer to the past

questions.explanation: Denotative words make direct, literal reference to things, so D is correct. Denotative meaning is the literal meaning of a word, the one entered in the dictionary; for example, dark denotes the absence of light. Options A, B and C have nothing to do with denotation: referring to the past, alphabetical listing and scientific use are unrelated ideas.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: Identify the misspelled word below
questions.explanation: The misspelled word is harrassment, option D; the correct spelling is harassment, with one r and two s's. Sphinx (A), embarrassment (B) and repertoire (C) are all spelt correctly. Embarrassment is the one with double r and double s, which is probably why people wrongly add an extra r to harassment.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: A dictionary aids vocabulary development by .....

options.c: Indicating the ways the words are pronounced
options.d: Indicating the context of usage and spelling

questions.explanation: A dictionary helps vocabulary grow by giving the meanings of words, showing how they are pronounced, and indicating their spelling and the contexts in which they are used. Since B, C and D are each true, A, all of these, is the correct choice; picking only one of them leaves out the others.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: Meaning in words is largely a matter of ........
questions.explanation: Meaning in words is largely a matter of agreement, option A, because the link between a word and what it stands for is a convention shared by speakers of a language, not something natural in the word itself. English accepts new words like vuvuzela once speakers agree to use them. Discord (B) is the opposite of shared meaning, and inherence (D) wrongly suggests meaning is built into the word. Standardised opinion (C) is not the term used.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: Identify the incorrectly spellled word below
questions.explanation: The misspelled word is souvenier, option B; the correct spelling is souvenir, ending in -ir, not -ier. It is one of the words English borrowed from French. Chauffeur (A), vagrant (C) and resinous (D) are all spelt correctly.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: As a prefix, ANTI- means
questions.explanation: The prefix anti- means against or opposed to, as in anti-social, or antibiotic (against the life forms that cause disease). Option C (dissimilar) is tempting because opposing something can suggest difference, but anti- expresses opposition, not just being different. A and B (congruent, similar) point the opposite way. Also take care not to confuse anti- with ante-, which means before.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: To be elected ................, candidates must have a solid background in law enforcement.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is sheriff, with one r and two f's, so A is correct. Option B doubles the r and drops an f, C drops an f, and D doubles both the r and the f, so all three are misspellings.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: Which of the following words is misspelled?
questions.explanation: The word in A is misspelt: the correct spelling is parachutist, ending in -ist, but option A has lost its final t. Communication, accommodation and swinging (B, C and D) are all spelt correctly, though accommodation is a common trap because it needs a double c and a double m.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: ................ is often called the awkward stage.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is adolescence, with -esc- in the middle and the noun ending -ence, and it is the stage of life often called awkward. Option A ends wrongly in -ense, B drops the e after the l, and C is a misspelt plural form (adolescents), which names the people rather than the stage of life.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: If you stay in water too long, your fingertips will
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is shrivel, ending in -el, and it means to wrinkle and shrink, which is what fingertips do after a long time in water. Option A adds an extra a, C reverses the last two letters, and D wrongly ends in -al.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: If neologism is taken to mean old words that have been given new meanings, which of the following is NOT an example of neologism?
questions.explanation: Brunch is not an old word with a new meaning: it is a blend, made by joining part of breakfast to part of lunch. Nice, lady and Waterloo are all old words whose meanings have shifted, for example Waterloo, once just a place name, now also means a final defeat.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: Words that habitually go together, such as "make a decision" or "heavy rain", are known as
questions.explanation: A collocation is a group of words that habitually occur together, so we say make a decision rather than do a decision. Option C (connotation) is the feeling or association attached to a single word, not a word grouping, and A and B (continuation, composition) are not terms for words that go together.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: In which of the following pairs does one word carry a negative connotation?
questions.explanation: Connotation is the feeling attached to a word beyond its literal meaning. Persistent is approving, but stubborn suggests an unreasonable refusal to change, so pair B contains a negative word. In A, C and D both words carry a positive feeling.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: The process of word formation where old words are given new meanings is called
questions.explanation: Neologism here means the process in which old words are given new meanings, such as nice, which once meant pretending to be good and now means kind, or Waterloo, which now means a defeat. Option B (coining) creates a word for a specific use, and C (blending) joins parts of two words, as in smog, so neither gives an existing word a new meaning. A (mixing) is not a word-formation process.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: A thesaurus is a
questions.explanation: A thesaurus is a dictionary of synonyms, and it is classed among specialised dictionaries, alongside scholarly and usage dictionaries. Options B, C and D (simplified, pictorial, phonetic) are not categories under which a thesaurus belongs.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: When a long word is shortened to make it less awkward in speech, it is said to be ...
questions.explanation: Clipping is the shortening of long words that are awkward in everyday speech, as in exam from examination and phone from telephone. Chopped, chipped and crimped (A, C and D) are not terms for word formation.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: Prefixes and suffixes are generally known as ----------
questions.explanation: Prefixes and suffixes together are called affixes, groups of letters added before or after a base (D). Option A, affixation, is the process of adding them, not the name of the elements themselves, while root and stem (B and C) are the bases the affixes attach to.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: ......occurs when the meaning of a word depends on its environment and usage.
questions.explanation: Contextual meaning is meaning worked out from the word's environment, using clues in the sentence such as paired words or parallelism (C). Connotation (A) is tempting, but it is the figurative meaning a word carries from feelings and experience, as in 'he's dark' meaning evil. Pronunciation and assimilation (B and D) concern sounds, not meaning.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: When the meaning of a word is considered in isolation, it is known as ......meaning.
questions.explanation: Denotative meaning is the literal, dictionary meaning of a word considered on its own, as in 'dark' meaning without light (D). Connotative meaning (C) comes from feelings, emotions and experience, so it is not meaning in isolation. Complex and objective (A and B) are not recognised types of word meaning.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: "un" in the word "unfaithful" is an example of a
questions.explanation: An affix added at the beginning of a word, like un- in unfaithful or unpleasant, is a prefix (B). A suffix (D) is added at the end of a word, like -ful in the same word. Subjunction and conjunct (A and C) are not names for word parts; a conjunct is a linking word.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: The words fax, prep, gents, zoo and ad are examples of which word-formation process?
questions.explanation: Clipping is shortening a long word that is awkward in speech, keeping only part of it, as in fax from facsimile or zoo from zoological garden (A). A blend (C) combines parts of two different words, like smog from smoke and fog, and an acronym (D) is formed from the initials of several words. Conversion (B) changes a word's class without changing its form.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: What is a thesaurus?

options.a: A dictionary of synonyms, which is a specialised dictionary
options.b: A general dictionary that gives the etymology of most words
options.c: A list of sources placed at the end of a research work
options.d: A brief summary of a book or article

questions.explanation: A thesaurus is a dictionary of synonyms, such as Roget International Thesaurus, and it counts as a specialised dictionary (A). Option B describes a general unabridged dictionary, which covers most words with details and etymology. A list of sources at the end of a work (C) is a bibliography, and a brief summary (D) is an abstract.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: The caverns were so damp that my skin felt
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is clammy, with a double m and a y, meaning unpleasantly damp and sticky (D). Option A, clamy, drops the second m, while B and C insert a b that does not belong in the word.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: Shakespeare is said to have used about how many words?
questions.explanation: Shakespeare is said to have used about 21,000 words. The figure 10,000 is the number that hardly any learner knows, and one million is the estimate of all English words.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: French words such as those about the kitchen, cooking and government entered English mainly through

options.b: the arrival of the Angles, Saxons and Jutes

questions.explanation: The Norman Conquest of 1066 AD brought French words about the kitchen, cooking, government and administration into English. The Renaissance is linked instead with Greek and Latin words, while the Angles, Saxons and Jutes brought Anglo-Saxon, the native base of English.

questions.topic: Vocabulary Development
questions.question: The words 'dilly-dally', 'nitty-gritty' and 'topsy-turvy' are formed by
questions.explanation: Reduplication doubles all or part of a word, usually changing one vowel or consonant, as in 'dilly-dally'. Blending is different: it joins part of one word to part of another, as in 'smog' from smoke and fog.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: _____ forms the building block of a sentence
questions.explanation: Words, option D, are the building blocks of a sentence: they combine to form phrases and clauses, which in turn form sentences. Sounds (A) and letters (B) are the building blocks of words, not sentences, and thoughts (C) are what a sentence expresses rather than what it is made of.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: Prepositions begin phrases that end with
questions.explanation: Prepositions begin phrases that end with either a noun or a pronoun, called the object of the preposition, as in under the table or at the bus-stop. So B is correct. Options A, C and D name word classes that do not serve as the object of a preposition.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: Words can be in any of the following forms except:
questions.explanation: A word can be simple (one unit, like table), compound (two words that can stand alone, like suitcase) or complex (a base with affixes, like unreliable). Compound-complex (option C) is not a word form; it is a type of sentence with two or more main clauses plus a subordinate clause. So C is the form a word cannot take.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: Interjections are usually punctuated with a/an ____________.
questions.explanation: Interjections express strong or sudden feeling and are usually punctuated with an exclamation mark, as in Ouch! That was painful and Hey! Watch out! So C is correct. A question mark (A) is for direct questions, a period (D) ends ordinary statements, and a comma (B) is used only after mild interjections, which is not the usual punctuation.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: The simple present tense is used to indicate
questions.explanation: The simple present tense is used when someone does something regularly or something goes on all the time, for example I jog every morning or The cock crows at dawn. So it signals regularity, option D. Option B, present, is tempting because of the name, but an action happening right now is the job of the present continuous. A completed past action (A) needs the simple past, and irregularity (C) is the opposite of what this tense shows.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: Free morphemes are sub-categorized into ---------------
questions.explanation: Free morphemes are words that can stand alone, and they fall into two groups: lexical morphemes, which carry content meaning (nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs such as boy, run, happy), and functional morphemes, which do grammatical work (articles, prepositions, conjunctions and pronouns such as the, of, and). So C is correct. Options A, B and D pair functional with a label (grammatical, descriptive) that is not the standard partner term; grammatical is just another word for functional, not a separate class.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: Which of the following are irregular nouns?
questions.explanation: Irregular nouns include those that change an internal vowel in the plural (man-men, woman-women, louse-lice, foot-feet, goose-geese, tooth-teeth) and those that change -f or -fe to -ves (leaf-leaves, wife-wives, half-halves). Since A, B and D all give genuine irregular plurals, C, all of these, is correct. Picking any single option leaves out equally valid examples.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: In the sentence "He arrived yesterday", the word "yesterday" is an
questions.explanation: In He arrived yesterday, the word yesterday is an adverb of time because it answers the question when did he arrive? So B is correct. An adverb of frequency (A) would answer how often, degree (C) would answer to what extent, and manner (D) would answer how, none of which fits yesterday.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: The word 'unhappily' contains-----------------
questions.explanation: Unhappily is built from three parts: the prefix un- (meaning not), the root happy, and the suffix -ly, which turns the adjective into an adverb, so A is correct. Option B is wrong because English words like this have no infix, and options C and D list two bases (stem and root) when unhappily has only one, and D also leaves out the prefix.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: I saw them across the road, the expression across the road can be described as a ------
questions.explanation: A prepositional phrase begins with a preposition and ends with a noun or pronoun called its object, as in under the bed and across the road, so D is correct. Option C, noun phrase, is tempting because the road is a noun phrase, but the whole expression is headed by the preposition across. Options A and B have a verb or adjective as the main word, which is not the case here.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: The category of words to which new words can always be added is called-------
questions.explanation: Open class words are word classes that readily accept new members, such as nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs, so new words like webinar or selfie can always be added. Closed class words (B) and grammatical words (C), such as prepositions and conjunctions, almost never gain new members. Suffixation words (D) is not a grammatical term.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: In "My mother cooks very well", the word "very" is an
questions.explanation: In My mother cooks very well, the word very tells us to what extent she cooks well, so it is an adverb of degree, option A. Option C (manner) is tempting because well on its own says how she cooks, but very only intensifies well. Options B and D (place, time) do not fit at all.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: The largest grammatical unit in English is the------and the smallest is the ---------
questions.explanation: The grammatical units run from the morpheme, through the word, phrase and clause, up to the sentence, so the sentence is the largest unit and the morpheme the smallest. Option A is wrong because the paragraph is a unit of writing, not of grammar. Options C and D name units that sit in the middle of the scale, since the word and the phrase are both bigger than the morpheme.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: What is the function of the word "boy" in the sentence: That boy is my cousin?
questions.explanation: In That boy is my cousin, the noun phrase that boy names what the sentence is about and comes before the verb, so boy is the subject of the verb is. Option A (object) would receive the action of a verb, but the linking verb is has no such object. D is wrong because that is a demonstrative determiner pointing to boy, not something boy completes, and B is not a grammatical function.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: The prefix un- in the word "unreliable" can be described as a/an --------- morpheme.
questions.explanation: The prefix un- is a derivational morpheme because it creates a new word with a different meaning: reliable becomes its opposite, unreliable. Option A is wrong because inflectional morphemes such as -s or -ed only mark grammar like number or tense without making a new word. Options B and C are wrong because un- cannot stand alone, so it is neither a free morpheme nor a lexical (content) word.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: Auxiliary verbs in English are classified into-------
questions.explanation: Auxiliary verbs are of two types: primary auxiliaries (have, be and do), which can also act as main verbs, and modal auxiliaries (can, will, shall, may, must), which never stand alone. Option A (modal and main) mixes an auxiliary type with main verbs, B (primary and secondary) invents a category, and D (regular and irregular) classifies verbs by how they form the past tense, not auxiliaries.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: Every complex word contains a/an --------------
questions.explanation: A morphologically complex word is formed by adding an affix, a group of letters placed before (prefix) or after (suffix) the base, as in unrepentant, disloyal and endearment. So every complex word contains an affix. Option C (prefix) is too narrow, since a word like fairness is complex with only a suffix, and A and B (verb, noun) are word classes, not parts of a word.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: In the sentence "We bought John a guitar", the phrase " a guitar" functions as-------- ?
questions.explanation: When a verb has two objects, the direct object answers what was bought, and the indirect object answers for or to whom. In We bought John a guitar, a guitar is what was bought, so it is the direct object, and John is the indirect object (option C). Options A and D (complements) would describe or rename the object or the subject, which a guitar does not do.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: One of the following does not describe a noun:

options.a: can be in past or present tense

questions.explanation: Tense belongs to verbs, not nouns, so a noun is not something that can be in the past or present tense, and A is correct. A noun can take a plural, have a possessive form, and be proper or common, so B, C and D all describe nouns properly.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: The base word in "Educational" is
questions.explanation: Educational is built by affixation: the root educate takes the suffix -ion to give education, and then the suffix -al to give educational, so the base is educate. Options B, C and D are only fragments of letters or a suffix and cannot stand alone as words, so none of them is the base.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: Nouns can be subclassified in the following ways except one.
questions.explanation: Nouns are subclassified in three pairs: proper and common, count and non-count, and concrete and abstract. Possessive is a form that a noun can take (girl's, girls'), just as singular and plural are forms, so possessive and non-possessive is not a subclass. B, C and D are all genuine subclasses of nouns.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: Which of these does not belong in this group?
questions.explanation: Lagos, John and Kaduna are proper nouns, each naming a particular place or person, and so they begin with capital letters. Mathematics is a common noun naming a general field of study, so B does not belong with the others.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: In the sentence "Mr. Dokunboh donated some books", the phrase "some books" is the
questions.explanation: In Mr. Dokunboh donated some books, some books receives the action of the verb and answers the question what was donated, so it is the direct object. Option B (indirect object) would apply only to a receiver such as the school in donated some books to the school, and C is wrong because Mr. Dokunboh, not the books, performs the action.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: When an adjective is placed before a noun, it is said to be in what position?
questions.explanation: An adjective placed before the noun it qualifies, as in the beautiful woman, is attributive, whereas one linked to the noun by a verb, as in the food is delicious, is predicative. Options A, B and D (superlative, comparative, positive) are degrees of comparison, which describe the form of an adjective, not its position.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: ----------------- words involve two or more independent words.
questions.explanation: Compound words are made of two or more words that can each stand independently, such as suitcase or blackboard. Option D (complex) is tempting, but a complex word contains an affix, as in unhappy, rather than two independent words. A simple word (C) has only one morpheme, and compound-complex (B) is a type of sentence, not a word type.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: Grammar is broadly classified into----------
questions.explanation: Grammar is divided into morphology, the study of how words are formed, and syntax, the study of how words are arranged into phrases, clauses and sentences. Option D names phonology (the sound system) and semantics (meaning), which are other areas of language study, not branches of grammar. Option A is not the standard division, and B mixes a unit with a vague term.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: Which of the following sentences makes use of an intransitive verb?
questions.explanation: An intransitive verb takes no object, and in The baby cried the verb cried has nothing after it receiving the action. Options A and B are transitive, since bought takes the object a car and ate takes the object the food. Option C uses the linking verb is with a complement, not an action verb without an object.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: In the sentence 'The young lady thanked Mr Dokubo', the phrase 'Mr Dokubo' functions as a/an ...
questions.explanation: In The young lady thanked Mr Dokubo, Mr. Dokubo receives the action of the transitive verb thanked, which makes it the direct object. Option B (indirect object) would need a second object that the action is done for or to, and A (complement) would need the phrase to refer to the same person as the subject.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: In the sentence: "They came late because of the heavy rain", the phrase the heavy rain is called?
questions.explanation: The heavy rain is built around the head noun rain, with the determiner the and the adjective heavy describing it, so it is a noun phrase. Option D is tempting because the phrase follows because of, but the prepositional phrase is the whole group because of the heavy rain, while the heavy rain on its own is the noun phrase inside it.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: A verb which always occurs with an object is a/an \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ verb.
questions.explanation: A transitive verb lets the action pass from the subject to an object, as in The man shut the door, so it always occurs with an object. Option A (intransitive) is the opposite, with no object, and B and D are helping verbs that accompany main verbs rather than taking objects themselves.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: The grammatical elements will, shall, could, should can and may are known as ----- --------
questions.explanation: Will, shall, could, should, can and may are modal auxiliary verbs, helping verbs that cannot stand alone but combine with main verbs to express ability, permission or obligation. Options A and C classify main verbs by whether they take an object, and B is wrong because modals are helping verbs, not main verbs.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: Which tense do you use when you want to say that something is happening at the time you are speaking or writing
questions.explanation: The present continuous tense is used for something happening at the time you are speaking or writing, and it is formed with be plus the -ing form, as in I am dancing. Option C, the simple present, is for habits and regular events, A (present perfect) links a past action to the present, and B (future) looks ahead.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: The words tall, taller, tallest are examples of what kind of adjective?
questions.explanation: Tall, taller, tallest shows an adjective that can be expressed in degrees, just like big, bigger, biggest or very big, so it is a gradable adjective (D). Option C, non-gradable, is the opposite: it covers absolute qualities such as perfect, unique or fatal that cannot be graded. A and B are not classes of adjective.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: The part of a word to which other elements can be added is called--------
questions.explanation: The root (or stem) is the part of a word to which other elements are attached; affixation adds prefixes and suffixes to a root word. Options A and D are the elements that get added, not the part they are added to, and B, a phrase, is a group of words rather than part of a word.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: In the sentence 'She walks briskly', the word 'briskly' is a/an ...
questions.explanation: In 'She walks briskly', the word briskly tells how the walking is done, so it is an adverb of manner (B). An adverb of frequency (A) would tell how often, place (C) would tell where, and degree (D) would tell to what extent.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: Grammatical hierarchy in English is structured in which of the following ways?

options.a: sentence, phrase, clause, word and morpheme.
options.b: morpheme, word, clause, phrase and sentence.
options.c: sentence, clause, phrase, word and sentence.
options.d: morpheme, word, phrase, clause and sentence.

questions.explanation: The grammatical units rank from smallest to largest as morpheme, word, phrase, clause and sentence, so D is correct. Option A reverses the order, B wrongly puts the clause before the phrase, and C reverses the order and repeats 'sentence'.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: In the sentence 'They lost some extremely valuable documents in the fire', the expression 'extremely valuable' is an example of a/an ...
questions.explanation: In 'extremely valuable documents', the adjective valuable is the head word, modified by the adverb extremely, and the whole phrase describes the noun documents, so it is an adjective phrase (A). Option D is tempting because extremely is an adverb, but it is not the head of the phrase, and B would need a noun as the head.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: In the sentence 'Mr Dokunboh thanked the lady', the phrase 'the lady' is the ...
questions.explanation: In 'Mr. Dokunboh thanked the lady', the lady receives the action of the verb, so she is the direct object (A). Option C is wrong because Mr. Dokunboh, who does the thanking, is the subject. Option B, the indirect object, would answer 'to or for whom', and there is only one object in this sentence.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: In the sentence 'Tade travelled to Ibadan', the phrase 'to Ibadan' functions as an ...
questions.explanation: In 'Tade travelled to Ibadan', the phrase to Ibadan tells where Tade travelled, so it is an adverb of place (B). It does not answer how (manner, A), how often (frequency, C) or when (time, D).

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: Lexical and functional morphemes are sub-groups of---------
questions.explanation: Morphemes are first divided into free morphemes, which can stand alone as words, and bound morphemes, which must attach to a root. Free morphemes are then sub-grouped into lexical morphemes (content words like nouns, verbs and adjectives) and functional morphemes (grammar words like prepositions and conjunctions), so A is correct. Option D is wrong because bound morphemes are affixes such as prefixes and suffixes, and stems and roots (B, C) are not the parent category either.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: How many forms does state-of-being verbs and action verbs have
questions.explanation: Apart from the verb be, which has eight forms, state-of-being verbs and action verbs usually have five forms: the base, the third person singular present, the past tense, the past participle and the -ing form. So A is correct. Two forms (C) is too few, while seven and nine (B and D) are more than any ordinary English verb has.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: The study of the arrangement of constituents within a sentence is called-------
questions.explanation: Syntax studies how words are arranged and combined into phrases, clauses and sentences, which is exactly what the question describes (B). Grammar (A) is too broad, since it covers both how words are formed and how they are combined. Morphology (D) studies the internal structure of words, and graphology (C) deals with the writing system.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: Mr. Dokunboh thanked the lady. (Note: intended underline is "the lady")
questions.explanation: In 'Mr. Dokunboh thanked the lady', the lady receives the action of the verb, so she is the direct object (D). Option A is wrong because Mr. Dokunboh, who does the thanking, is the subject. Option C, the indirect object, would answer 'to or for whom', and there is only one object here.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: One of these is not a Correlative conjunctions
questions.explanation: The correlative conjunctions are both...and, either...or, just as...so, neither...nor, not only...but (also) and whether...or. 'Even...then' is not a recognised correlative pair, so A is the odd one out, while B, C and D are all genuine pairs.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: The man jogs regularly.
questions.explanation: In 'The man jogs regularly', the word regularly tells how often the man jogs, so it is an adverb of frequency (D). Manner (C) would answer how, time (B) would answer when, and place (A) would answer where.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: One of these is not a type of Pronoun
questions.explanation: The types of pronoun include personal, possessive, interrogative, relative, demonstrative, reciprocal, reflexive, intensive and indefinite pronouns. There is no class called refractive pronouns; the word is a distortion of reflexive, so B is the answer. Possessive, interrogative and reciprocal pronouns (A, C and D) are all genuine types, reciprocal ones being each other and one another.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: Wow! Oh no! and Watch it! are ___________
questions.explanation: Interjections are words or phrases that express strong feelings, emotions or exclamation, like Wow! Oh no! and Watch it! (B). Prepositions and conjunctions (A and D) show relationships or join words, and nouns (C) name things, so none of them expresses sudden emotion in this way.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: Which of the following phrases contains an indefinite article?
questions.explanation: The articles are the (definite) and a or an (indefinite), so 'A big fat hen' contains the indefinite article a (B). Option C uses the definite article the, while that (A) is a demonstrative and my (D) is a possessive determiner.

questions.topic: Grammar I: Word Classes and Phrases
questions.question: Grammar is categorized into two major sections, namely;
questions.explanation: Grammar is traditionally divided into morphology, the study of how words are formed, and syntax, the study of how words are combined into sentences (D). Option B is wrong because semantics is the study of meaning, not a branch of grammar, and C is wrong because phonetics studies speech sounds. Lexis (A) refers to vocabulary rather than grammatical structure.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: One of these is not a minor sentence
questions.explanation: Minor sentences are meaningful but grammatically incomplete structures whose missing parts can be recovered from context, such as Gatekeeper wanted, No fuel and No vacancy (options A, B and C). God bless you, option D, has a subject (God) and a finite verb (bless), so it is a complete major sentence, which makes it the one that is not a minor sentence.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: A simple sentence has

options.a: two clauses and no finite verb
options.b: one clause and contains only one finite verb
options.c: two clauses and contains only one finite verb
options.d: one clause and contains only two finite verb

questions.explanation: A simple sentence makes a single statement, has only one clause and contains only one finite verb, as in The boy killed the snake, so B is correct. Options A and C describe two clauses, which would make the sentence compound, and D gives two finite verbs, which also means more than one clause.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: Another name for Adjective Clause is
questions.explanation: A subordinate clause that modifies a noun the way an adjective does is called an adjectival clause or relative clause, because it is usually introduced by a relative pronoun such as who, whom, whose, which or that. So D is correct. A restrictive clause (B) is only one sub-type of relative clause, the defining kind, not another name for all adjective clauses, and A and C are not grammatical terms.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: Interrogative sentences \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_
questions.explanation: Sentences are classified by function into declarative, interrogative, imperative and exclamatory, and an interrogative sentence asks a question, such as What were you doing this morning? So A is correct. Option B describes the exclamatory sentence, C describes the declarative, and D describes the imperative.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: One of these is not a Type of Subordinate Clauses
questions.explanation: Subordinate clauses are classified by form into the finite clause (the verb changes with person, number and tense), the non-finite clause (the verb form stays the same) and the verbless clause (no verb at all). There is no such thing as an infinite clause in grammar, so A is the one that does not belong. Options B, C and D are all genuine types.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: Sentences can be grouped into all but one of the following types
questions.explanation: Sentences are grouped by function into four types: declarative (statements), interrogative (questions), imperative (directives) and exclamatory (strong emotion). Interlocutory is a legal and conversational term, not a sentence type, so D is the odd one out. Options A, B and C all belong to the list.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: Declarative sentences end with a/an \_\_\_\_\_
questions.explanation: A declarative sentence is a statement, and it ends with a full stop or period, as in Our organisation trades in petroleum products. Option A (exclamation point) ends excited or emotional statements, D (question mark) ends direct questions, and C (comma) cannot end a sentence at all.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: The major components of a sentence are

options.c: a main clause and a subordinate clause

questions.explanation: Every sentence has two major components: the subject, which names the person or thing being talked about, and the predicate, which says something about that subject, as in Birds (subject) fly (predicate). Options C and D (main/subordinate or independent/dependent clauses) describe how complex sentences are built, not the basic parts every sentence has, and A (nouns and adjectives) are word classes, not sentence parts.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: A finite clause contains one of the following
questions.explanation: A finite clause contains a finite verb, a verb form that changes with number, person and tense (visit, visits, visited), so C is correct. Option D (a verb that remains unchanging) describes a non-finite clause, B (no verb) describes a verbless clause, and A (two or more verbs) is not a defining feature of any clause type.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: Which one of the following is a simple sentence

options.a: Ngozi was at the scene, but she didn't witness the accident.
options.d: The teacher asked a difficult question and no student could answer it.

questions.explanation: A simple sentence makes a single statement with only one finite verb, and The boy killed the snake is exactly that. Options A and D are compound sentences, with two clauses joined by but and and. Option B, No smoking, is a minor sentence because it lacks a subject and a finite verb.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: One of the following is not an imperative sentence
questions.explanation: Oh, my goodness! is an exclamatory sentence, expressing strong emotion, so it is not imperative. Get out!, Have a drink. and Look out! (A, C and B) are imperatives, because they command, invite and warn.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: Which clause patterns is reflected in this sentence : Kofi became the president.
questions.explanation: Kofi became the president follows the SVC pattern: Kofi is the subject, became is the verb, and the president is the subject complement because it refers to the same person as the subject. Option A (SVOC) would need an object as well as a complement, and C (SVOO) would need two objects, which this sentence does not have.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: In the sentence "She hung onto his feet as if her life depended on it", the clause "as if her life depended on it" is what type of clause?
questions.explanation: In She hung onto his feet as if her life depended on it, the clause as if her life depended on it modifies the verb hung by saying how she held on, so it is an adverbial clause of manner. Options B and C would need the clause to describe a noun, which it does not, and D is not a recognised clause type.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: A simple sentence occurring by itself can also be called
questions.explanation: A simple sentence that stands by itself has one subject and one predicate, which is exactly what a clause is, so it can also be called a clause (C). Options A and B are not grammatical units at all, and verbal (D) describes a form of the verb, not a sentence.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: A complex sentence has

options.a: one independent clause and one or more dependent clauses.
options.b: one independent clause and one dependent clause
options.c: two independent clauses and one dependent clause
options.d: two independent clauses and one or more dependent clauses

questions.explanation: A complex sentence has one independent (main) clause and one or more dependent (subordinate) clauses, so A is correct. Option B is too narrow because a complex sentence may have more than one dependent clause. C and D describe sentences with two independent clauses, which are compound-complex sentences.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: How many basic clause patterns are there in the English simple sentence?
questions.explanation: There are seven basic clause patterns in the English simple sentence: SV, SVO, SVC, SVA, SVOO, SVOC and SVOA. So B is correct, and 4, 8 and 6 (A, C and D) are the wrong counts.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: Which of these words cannot be used to introduce an adverb clause?
questions.explanation: Nevertheless is a conjunctive adverb, which links two independent clauses of equal status rather than making one clause dependent, so it cannot introduce an adverb clause (B). Although, when and if (A, C and D) are genuine subordinating conjunctions that introduce adverb clauses.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: Which clause patterns is reflected in this sentence : The man bought his wife a present.
questions.explanation: In 'The man bought his wife a present', the man is the subject, bought is the verb, his wife is the indirect object and a present is the direct object, which is the SVOO pattern (A). SVOC (B) would need a complement describing the object, and SVOA (C) would need an adverbial of time or place, neither of which appears here.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: Identify the imperative sentence below

options.c: Did you take the bus home?
options.d: She walked quickly to the bus stop.

questions.explanation: An imperative sentence gives a directive such as a command, instruction or piece of advice, usually with the subject 'you' understood, so 'Take the bus home.' is the imperative (A). Option B is an exclamatory sentence expressing strong feeling, C is an interrogative because it asks a question, and D is a declarative that simply makes a statement.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: Which of these sentences has a plural compound subject

options.a: The man and his wife were present.
options.b: Hot lemonade and honey is good for a cold.
options.c: The MD and Chief Executive Officer of the company was introduced
options.d: Waiter is the rice and beans ready?

questions.explanation: A compound subject joined by 'and' is plural, so 'The man and his wife' takes the plural verb were (A). In B, C and D the members are thought of as a single unit, such as one drink (lemonade and honey), one dish (rice and beans) or one person holding two titles, so those compound subjects are singular.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: One of these is not a basic clause pattern in the English simple sentence
questions.explanation: The seven basic clause patterns are SV, SVO, SVC, SVA, SVOO, SVOC and SVOA. SVCC is not one of them because a clause does not take two complements in this way, so B is the answer. SVA, SVOA and SVO (A, C and D) are all genuine patterns.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: She hung onto his feet as if her life depended on it. What type of clause is 'as if her life depended on it'?
questions.explanation: In 'as if her life depended on it', the clause modifies the verb hung by telling how she held on, so it is an adverbial clause of manner (C). An adjectival clause (A) would modify a noun, not a verb, and 'relative clause of manner' (D) is not a recognised clause type. Option B is not a clause type either.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: Which clause patterns is reflected in this sentence : Jesus wept.
questions.explanation: In 'Jesus wept', Jesus is the subject and wept is the verb, with no object, complement or adverbial, so the pattern is SV (A). SVO (C) would need something receiving the action, and SVC and SVA (B and D) would need a complement or an adverbial after the verb.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a coordinating conjunction used to join the clauses of a compound sentence?
questions.explanation: So that is a subordinating conjunction that makes one clause depend on another, which produces a complex sentence, so it is not used in compound sentences (A). Compound sentences use coordinating conjunctions such as and, but, or, nor, for and yet, which is why B, C and D are not the answer.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: Which clause patterns is reflected in this sentence : The priest pronounced the couple man and wife.
questions.explanation: In 'The priest pronounced the couple man and wife', the priest is the subject, pronounced is the verb, the couple is the object and man and wife is the object complement, which describes the same people as the object. That is the SVOC pattern (A). SVOO (D) would need two different objects, such as a receiver and a thing given, while SVA and SVC (B and C) have no object at all.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: Which of the following is a non-finite clause?
questions.explanation: A non-finite clause has a verb that does not change for number, person or tense, and it often has no subject; "having died down" fits this exactly. "While in prison" is tempting, but it has no verb at all, so it is a verbless clause, not a non-finite one.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: In the sentence "While in prison, he wrote a novel", the clause "while in prison" is best described as a
questions.explanation: "While in prison" has no verb and no subject of its own; the missing subject is understood from the main clause (he), which makes it a verbless clause. It is not a non-finite clause, because a non-finite clause still contains a verb form such as "being repaired" or "to leave".

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: What does the sentence "The students who arrived late were locked out" mean?

options.a: None of the students arrived on time
options.b: All the students were locked out
options.c: The students came late because they were locked out
options.d: Only the students who came late were locked out

questions.explanation: Without commas, "who arrived late" is a defining relative clause: it identifies which students are meant, so only some of them, the late ones, were locked out. If the clause were set off by commas ("The students, who arrived late, were locked out"), it would be non-defining and would mean that all the students were locked out.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: Which relative pronoun can NOT be used to introduce a non-defining relative clause?
questions.explanation: A non-defining clause adds extra information about a noun that is already known, is set off by paired commas, and does not allow "that" (so "Chike, that had never been ..." is wrong). "Which" is a tempting choice, but it can introduce a non-defining clause, for example "The car, which was new, broke down".

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: In the sentence "The fact that she is not here worries everyone in the department", the clause "that she is not here" functions as
questions.explanation: The noun clause "that she is not here" explains what "the fact" is, so it stands in apposition to that noun. It is not a direct object, because it does not come after a verb as the thing acted on; it is attached to the noun "fact".

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: A sentence that has two or more main clauses and at least one subordinate clause is called a
questions.explanation: A compound-complex sentence combines the features of both types: two or more main clauses plus at least one subordinate clause. A complex sentence is the closest wrong choice, but it has only one main clause with one or more subordinate clauses.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: A major sentence made up of three or more independent clauses is known as a
questions.explanation: When three or more independent clauses are joined together, the result is a multiple sentence. A compound sentence is the nearest wrong answer, but it joins two independent clauses with coordinating conjunctions or conjunctive adverbs.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: The imperative sentence "Let me see." expresses which type of directive?
questions.explanation: "Let me see" is the speaker thinking aloud, which is the meditating type of directive. It may look like "Let's go by bus", but that one is suggesting, because it proposes an action to others; "Suit yourself" is permitting and "Have mercy" is pleading.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: Which clause pattern does the sentence "The plane took off at eight o'clock" show?
questions.explanation: "The plane" is the subject, "took off" is the verb and "at eight o'clock" is an adverbial of time, giving SVA. SVOA is tempting, but there is no object here, since nothing receives the action of taking off.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: Choose the correct verb: Either you or I ____ responsible for the shop in Balogun market.
questions.explanation: With "either ... or" joining mixed members, the verb follows the concord of proximity and agrees with the nearest subject, which is "I", so "am" is correct. "Are" is the tempting choice because "you" takes "are", but "you" is not the member closest to the verb.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: Choose the correct verb: The Manager, together with all his staff, ____ at the bank's end-of-year party in Victoria Island.
questions.explanation: A singular subject followed by "together with" still takes a singular verb, because the phrase after "together with" is not part of the subject; the subject is "The Manager". "Were" is tempting because "all his staff" sounds plural, but those words do not control the verb.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?

options.a: The number of students in the department is rising.
options.b: The number of students in the department are rising.
options.c: A number of students is absent from the test.
options.d: A number of students was absent from the test.

questions.explanation: "The number of" refers to a single figure, so it takes a singular verb (is), while "a number of" means several and takes a plural verb (were or are). The sentence with "The number of students ... are rising" is the most tempting wrong option, but it wrongly treats "the number" as plural.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: "The jury has reached a verdict" takes a singular verb because the jury is thought of as one unit. This type of agreement with collective nouns is called
questions.explanation: Collective nouns follow notional concord: the verb is singular when the group acts as a unit and plural when its members act as individuals ("The jury are still arguing"). Concord of proximity is a different rule, used when a verb agrees with the nearest member of an "either ... or" or "neither ... nor" subject.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: "Returning home late one night, a snake bit Olu." This sentence contains which fault?
questions.explanation: The phrase "Returning home late one night" should modify Olu, but it sits next to "a snake", making it seem the snake was returning home; this is a dangling modifier. It can be corrected as "Returning home late one night, Olu was bitten by a snake". It is not a comma splice, because a comma splice joins two complete sentences with only a comma.

questions.topic: Grammar II: Clauses and Sentences
questions.question: A student writes "Because I was hungry." as a complete sentence. This is an example of
questions.explanation: "Because" makes the clause dependent, so "Because I was hungry." is an incomplete thought standing alone, which is a sentence fragment and is unacceptable. A minor sentence such as "No vacancy." is tempting, but a minor sentence is acceptable because its missing parts can be recovered from the context.

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: Weeding as a library term means
questions.explanation: In library work, weeding means removing outdated, damaged or no-longer-useful books from the collection so the shelves hold current, relevant material, which is option D. The word borrows the gardening idea of pulling out unwanted plants. Options A and B are ordinary cleaning jobs and C is about controlling users, none of which is what librarians mean by weeding.

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: Books are placed on reserve to

options.b: To prevent them from getting to unregistered users
options.c: To preserve them for serious-minded library-going students
options.d: To facilitate a rapid and wider circulation of scarce materials among users

questions.explanation: Books are placed on reserve so that scarce or heavily demanded material can circulate quickly among many users instead of being borrowed by one person for weeks, which is option D. Reserved items are rare and valuable, are not placed on long loan and must be consulted in the reading room. Options A, B and C are wrong because reserving is about sharing access, not protecting books from wear, keeping them from unregistered users or saving them for only serious students.

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: The circulation section of the library deals with

options.b: The distribution of books among affiliated libraries
options.d: The cataloguing and classification of acquired materials

questions.explanation: The circulation section handles the lending and return of books, so A is correct; the circulation desk is also where you can ask for help locating a book. Option B is interlibrary lending, a separate service, while acquiring new materials (C) and cataloguing and classifying them (D) are done by the acquisitions and cataloguing sections.

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: Reference books are those

options.d: They contain a wealth of materials which cut across various disciplines

questions.explanation: Reference books such as dictionaries, encyclopaedias and handbooks are consulted for specific facts rather than read from cover to cover, so libraries keep them in the reference section and they cannot be borrowed, which is option B. Option A is too narrow, C (bulky) is irrelevant, and D describes general collections rather than what makes a book a reference book.

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: The encyclopedia is

options.a: A book or a set of books on Britain
options.b: A book or a set of books on America
options.c: A book or a set of books on one or all branches of knowledge
options.d: A book or a set of books compiled by chambers

questions.explanation: An encyclopaedia is a book or set of books that gives background and current information on one or all branches of knowledge, so C is correct. Encyclopaedias can be general, like Britannica or Americana, or subject-based, like an encyclopaedia of philosophy. Options A, B and D mistake the names Britannica, Americana and Chambers for the definition; those are just titles or publishers.

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: Books put in the reserve section of the library

options.a: Are intended for use by library staff only
options.c: Can be borrowed for a full semester
options.d: Out of the reach of students

questions.explanation: Books in the reserve section cannot be borrowed out of the library, so B is correct. They are rare or valuable, kept on closed access, and must be consulted in the reading room, although photocopying is allowed. Option C is wrong because reserve items are never placed on long loan, and they are meant for students, not staff only (A), so they are not out of students' reach (D).

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: One of the attributes of information is .................
questions.explanation: Relevance, option C, is one of the attributes of good information, alongside availability, accuracy, reliability and timeliness. Citation (A) and printing (B) are things done with information, not qualities of it, and non-reliability (D) is the opposite of reliability, which is a required attribute.

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: An example of a specialized dictionary is ..........
questions.explanation: The Dictionary of American Slang, option C, is a specialized dictionary because it is compiled for a particular purpose and covers only one area of vocabulary. Other specialized examples include the Dictionary of the Yoruba Language and the Dictionary of Modern Politics. Webster's (A) and the Oxford English Dictionary (B) are general dictionaries, so D, none, is also wrong.

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: A secondary source is one that ............. and ................ a primary source.
questions.explanation: A secondary source analyzes, critiques, reviews or explains a primary source, and is written by scholars who have studied the original and drawn their own conclusions. So D, analyzes and explains, matches the definition. Options A and B use words like disqualify and manipulates that are not part of the definition, so C, all, is also wrong.

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: Radio, Tape-recorder, Gramophone and Audio cassette player are examples of ............
questions.explanation: Radio, tape-recorder, gramophone and audio cassette player all deliver information through sound alone, so they are audio materials, option B; in the University of Lagos library they are found in the Music Library. Visual materials (A), such as maps and pictures, appeal to the eye only, audio-visual materials (C) like television and LCD projectors combine sound and picture, and electronic material (D) is too broad a label for this group.

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: Article/journal search can be carried out or done in these sections of the library
questions.explanation: Journal and article searches are done in the Serials section, which holds publications issued in successive parts such as journals, newspapers and magazines, and in the E-library, where electronic journals and databases are accessed. So A is correct. The Cataloguing section (B) and Acquisition section (C) are back-office units that process materials, and the University Librarian's office (D) is administrative.

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: Index may be published as part of a book or separately
questions.explanation: The statement is true, option D: an index may be published as part of a book, like the index at the back of that book, or separately, like a periodical index that stands alone. Options A, B and C treat the statement as wholly or partly false, but both forms of publication really exist, with no qualification needed.

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: .............. is consulted mostly by speech makers and writers
questions.explanation: A book of quotation supplies quotations on various subjects by particular authors, and it is mostly consulted by speech makers and writers, so A is correct. A biographical book (B) gives facts about individuals, a manual (C) explains how to do things, and a book of reference (D) is too general to be the answer.

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: ................. are allowed access into Gandhi Library
questions.explanation: Access to the University of Lagos Research and Bibliographic Department, known as the Gandhi Library, is strictly for researchers and postgraduate students, so B is correct. Undergraduates are admitted only on presenting a letter from a head of department, supervisor or course lecturer. Options A and C name groups that are not the ones admitted, and D is wrong because a specific group is named.

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: Publications issued in successive parts, at regular intervals, and intended to be continued indefinitely are .......
questions.explanation: A publication issued in successive parts, at regular intervals, and usually intended to continue indefinitely is a serial, so A, serials collection, is correct. Newspapers, magazines, journals, indexes and abstracts are examples. Serials report and collective report (C and D) are not library terms, and B is wrong because the definition fits a serial exactly.

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: Africana materials are not loanable and users are not permitted to take them out of gandhi library
questions.explanation: The statement is true, option B: Africana materials in the Gandhi Library (the Research and Bibliographic Department) are not loanable and cannot be taken out of that department. They may only be consulted there, although photocopying is allowed. Options A, C and D treat the statement as wholly or partly false, which is not correct.

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: Example of Audio-visual materials is
questions.explanation: Television, option C, is an audio-visual material because it combines sound and picture; other examples are LCD projectors, computers and VCD players. A map (A) is a visual material only, while a book (B) and a journal (D) are print resources.

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: The person who provides reference services is called...........
questions.explanation: The librarian whose job is to help users find information and answer enquiries at the reference section is the reference librarian, option A; the title describes the service offered. A chief librarian (B) and a university librarian (C) are titles for the overall head of the library, and a library officer (D) is a general staff designation rather than the person who provides reference services.

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: ................. is not a type of abstract
questions.explanation: The three recognized types of abstract are the indicative, informative and evaluative abstracts. Review abstract (option C) is not one of them, so it is the answer. Options A, B and D are all genuine types.

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: The Research and Bibliographic section of the library houses ..........
questions.explanation: The Research and Bibliographic Department, known as the Gandhi Library, holds research materials including PhD theses and old and current newspapers dating back to 1930, so B, which combines A and D, is correct. Choosing A or D alone leaves out the other holding. Law books (C) are not what this department is known for.

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: Reference materials include the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Journals are serials, meaning they are published in successive parts at regular intervals, so they are not classed as reference materials. Reference materials are things like dictionaries, encyclopaedias, indexes, biographies, handbooks and manuals, which you consult for quick facts. That is why A, C and D are all reference materials and B is the exception.

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: The ability to recognize when information is needed is called .........
questions.explanation: Information literacy is the ability to locate, retrieve, evaluate and apply information, and it includes recognising when information is needed (this is the American Library Association's definition). Option B (data) means raw facts, C (information explosion) is the rapid growth in the amount of information available, and A is not a recognised term.

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: The main kinds of electronic materials in most libraries are:
questions.explanation: Electronic library materials are things like electronic books, electronic journals, electronic images and full-text records from the internet, so e-books and e-periodicals fit. Pamphlets, cassettes and videotapes (in B and D) are print or audio-visual items, not electronic ones, and option C (cards, newspapers) lists print formats.

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: Generally, information sources are divided into which of the following categories?
questions.explanation: Information sources fall into two categories: primary sources (first-hand accounts such as original research reports, diaries or novels) and secondary sources (works that analyse or explain a primary source). So the correct choice is A, which combines C and D. Choosing C or D alone leaves out the other category, and B (tertiary) is not one of the two categories.

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: ............. collections are not expected to be read from cover to cover like books
questions.explanation: Reference collections, such as dictionaries, encyclopaedias, indexes and fact sources, are consulted for specific pieces of information, so they are not meant to be read from cover to cover. Option D (Africana) is a research collection of materials on Africa, and its books and theses are studied like other books. Option B (abstract) is only one type of reference source, not a library collection, and C (Americana) is the name of an encyclopaedia, not a collection.

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: The two sources of information are:
questions.explanation: The two sources of information are primary and secondary. Primary sources give first-hand accounts such as original research, letters or novels, while secondary sources analyse, review or explain a primary source. Option C (print and electronic) is tempting because it is a real division of library resources by format, but it divides them by medium, not by kind of source. A and B are informal groupings, not the standard categories.

questions.topic: Understanding the Library and Information Resources
questions.question: Publications conveying recent original research and observation are known as..............
